speechtext:

With federal spending up by 127 per cent in the past six years which has led to a 100 per cent growth in our money supply in the same period and to 55 per cent inflation while real growth was only 31.6 per cent, and with tourist activity especially in the nation's capital needing a stimulant, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke):

PROPOSAL TO CURTAIL CIGARETTE SMOKING-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the statement made yesterday by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to the effect that the smoking of cigarettes is more dangerous than the normal consumption of saccharin, especially in terms of causing cancer, and in view of the action taken by the Minister with respect to saccharin, I wish to present a motion under Standing Order 43. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
That this House calls on the Government to present to parliament a comprehensive program designed to curtail cigarette smoking in Canada, and that such a program include a ban on all cigarette advertising, adequate and visible health warnings on all cigarette packages, higher taxes on cigarettes containing high levels of tar or nicotine, and special measures to achieve a cleaner environment for all Canadians.

subtopic: REASON MINISTER DOES NOT FORBID USE OF TOBACCO
REASON MINISTER DOES NOT FORBID USE OF TOBACCO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to address a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare about his decision to ban saccharin.
Since saccharin has been used for many years either by diabetics or cardiacs and that in the minister's opinion no cancer case has been detected so far and since it has been stated on many occasions that the cigarette was a carcinogenic agent, could the minister tell the House on what grounds he decided to forbid the sale and use of saccharin and why he does not take any action against smoking since it has harmful effects on health?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REASON MINISTER DOES NOT FORBID USE OF TOBACCO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to answer the first part of the question, this decision has been made following a scientific study which lasted more than three years in my department and whose results were confirmed by a great number of international authorities invited to examine its findings.
On the second part of the question, I will say that there is a notable difference between cigarettes and saccharin since the latter is an additive in a great number of foods and drinks and plays no essential role while cigarettes are a substance consumed rather uniquely, so to speak, and it is not linked to consuming of other products. In addition it must be recognized that unfortunately cigarettes are part of our environment and condition of living and that it is not realistic to think that we could forbid their use as easily as saccharin.

The hon. member for St. John's East raises a point that has given the Chair and the House difficulties on previous occasions. There can be no doubt that ministers who, in good faith, seek further information before delivering an answer should be able to give the answer. I have always taken the attitude that a member should not be entitled to put supplementary questions but should withhold them until the answer is forthcoming from the minister. Then I would make an effort to recognize the right of hon. members to ask supplementary questions at that time.
However, the difficulty continues in that a minister who rejoins the House with the information is dependent, to a certain extent, on the ability of the hon. member to rise- which fair rotation on that day may not allow-or else attempt to do what the minister did today, that is, rise during the question period to answer an unasked question. I do not really think I or anyone else can speculate on the reasons several thousand foreign exchange traders could have on any particular day for taking positions with regard to the Canadian dollar. subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY

speakeroldname: Mr. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, four weeks from Saturday will be the sixtieth anniversary of one of the most significant events in the history of our great country. I am referring to the battle of Vimy Ridge which took place on April 9, 1917, and which historians have declared to be the day on which Canada became a nation. I am proud to say that this memorable occasion will be officially marked by a service at the Vimy Memorial and that 24 survivors of the Canadian Corps who took part in that glorious victory will be there to pay tribute to their fallen comrades.
These survivors come from all across Canada and were chosen to represent the warriors of Vimy by the Royal Canadian Legion and the National Council of Veterans Associations. I am honoured to be heading a party including so many of Canada's heroes who will be revisiting the site of their great triumph. With a couple of exceptions they are all over 80, but I know their love for Canada still burns as fiercely as it did 60 years ago when they stormed up Vimy Ridge a hundred thousand strong and turned the tide of defeat into the flood of victory.
This ceremony will commemorate a day when Canadians were united in a common cause: one Canada, glorious and free. Let us keep the faith with them.

subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to thank the minister for sending us a copy of his statement with regard to his visit along with 24 survivors most of whom are over 80 years of age. On April 9 they will be commemorating the battle of Vimy Ridge. Hon. members on this side of the House say to them, "Go with God's blessing."
The minister should be aware that it was around the same time in 1917 that the then prime minister of Canada thanked Canadian troops for the sacrifice they were making in the First World War. He assured them that the Canadian nation would always remember the sacrifice they had made and would always be committed to caring for veterans and their dependants. With all sincerity, I suggest that the minister consider some of the inequities which still remain in the veterans' charter with regard to World War I veterans. World War I

veterans who were incarcerated in prisoner of war camps are still not included in our prisoner of war compensation legislation. Here we are, 60 years later, and some veterans who served during the First World War cannot as yet qualify for war veterans' allowances unless they served for 365 days.
There is another glaring inequity of which the minister is aware, and that is that many veterans at age 80 who have widows live in fear. Those who fall within the category of having disability pensions of less than 48 per cent fear that their widows will be left without a widow's pension. The minister mentioned that they show a love for Canada, and I fully agree with him. I think the minister should remind the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) of that fact. With the threat of destruction of our national unity, their conduct in the First World War, the Second World War and the Korean conflict is an example of the comradeship that was shown regardless of race, creed or colour; it reminds us of the sacrifices they made to make Canada what it is today and the efforts we must make to preserve our national unity.
As a Newfoundlander, I hope the minister realizes that on July 1 in Newfoundland we celebrate the battle of Beaumont-Hamel. Perhaps the minister can find the time to join in the ceremony in memory of those who suffered and died and lie in the graves of Europe.
I can only repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the minister goes with God's blessing and I hope he will reflect, upon his return, and show that we appreciate the sacrifices made by those veterans.

subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should first of all like to wish the distinguished and gallant minister well on his trip to Vimy Ridge. I hope he will carry with him not only the good wishes of his own party but certainly the good wishes and admiration of all of us in the New Democratic Party.

subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
It is one of those occasions when we take pride in our veterans and express our appreciation for their efforts in keeping this country free.
The minister concluded his remarks today on a bit of a gushy note, yet I think it was a very appropriate bit of gush and perhaps we should be doing more of that. If the minister would excuse me, I would not mind doing a little gushing myself. As bad as war is, as horrible as war is, most of us who have been in war know that there is another side. Those of us who served in the armed forces, particularly in time of war, developed a comradeship, a sense of identity, a sense of loyalty and participation one with another. For instance, I was thinking it rather odd that the two people responding to the minister today are both Jews. One of the things that impressed me during the war was that questions of religion, race and colour broke down in the shared experience of preserving our free-
March 10, 1977

dom. It is that kind of spirit that is required in Canada today. It is for that reason that I welcome this occasion.
I am glad to see that the minister will be accompanied by survivors of Vimy Ridge. This is not only honour to the survivors but to all those thousands of Canadians who gave their lives for freedom. I hope their example will serve us well in Canada at this time when we face the difficult problem of keeping our country together.

subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BATTLE OF VIMY RIDGE RECOGNITION OF SIXTIETH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) for his statement recalling the great battle of Vimy and its 24 Canadian survivors. History does not say whether they were English or French-speaking Canadians, for that did not matter at the time. They were there in our country's defence and, at a certain point, they achieved unity in spite of the difficulties ,it presented at the time-I was only 3 or 4 years old-namely, the fact that French-speaking Canadians did not accept the draft too readily.
Nevertheless, French-speaking Canadians accepted courageously, open-heartedly to go overseas to defend our liberties, the rights that we now cherish. The minister's statement really touches me because I have a brother who is now 79 years old and even though he did not fight in the battle of Vimy, he was overseas, a soldier of the 22nd Regiment for 32 months as a volunteer. He wanted to serve Canada voluntarily and I am certain that he will be very happy when I get in touch with him tomorrow to let him know all the nice things the Minister of Veterans Affairs said today. He will be comforted and at the same time strengthened in a way by this patriotism he, like all the others, showed for our country.
Mr. Speaker, the minister's initiative in celebrating this event with fanfare by inviting the surviving Canadian soldiers of this battle deserves applause. There are enough disagreeable things that must be hushed up tactfully. When something nice happens, something that warms our heart like the minister's initiative today, we must commend him highly, and thank him on behalf of the soldiers who did their best to preserve the rights we still hold today.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I will simply point out that the minister talked about national unity. I concur with him and think that it warrants further discussion. National unity was strengthened during the war, cemented in a way by the spirit of patriotism which moved both English- and French-speaking Canadians.
Today, in 1977, the situation has changed, but we should work together with the same eagerness and heart and love for our native land so as to strengthen even more the national unity which will not be at the expense of English-speaking or French-speaking Canadians, but a national unity which will prove profitable to all Canadians. There are many other comments, which I could make, Mr. Speaker, but I must heartily tell the minister how grateful I am and thank him for

subsubtopic: SIXTY-FIVE YEARS OF AGE AND OVER CONTINGENT UPON RESIDENCE IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not take long. I want to emphasize and put forward further information which will show that some of the answers of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) were at best inaccurate and at worst an attempt to mislead this House in terms of the situation concerning spouses' allowances. At present the government of Canada will pay one spouse between the age of 60 and 65 a pension if the other spouse is already receiving the old age pension; but when the older spouse dies, the government cuts off that pension. Yesterday the Minister of National Health and Welfare suggested that our proposals with regard to spouses' allowances would cost in excess of $2 billion. I suggest that his response was totally unacceptable since in committee he suggested that the spouses' allowance program would cost a maximum of around $700,000.
The minister and government supporters tried to say that we cannot ask the government to increase its spending on the one hand but reduce expenditures on the other. You must remember that this is an inequitable situation, for the government has paid money to these people and they have become accustomed to a certain standard of living. Then, when there is a death in the family, the surviving spouse does not receive the allowance. I submit that the spouse needs the money to continue living in dignity.
How can the government's position be justified, in view of the most inefficient ways it uses money? Last year the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) wasted $740,000 in jet jaunts across the country. Information Canada was costing up to $10 million a year. In the Post Office the numerical strength of its membership has increased in the last eight years from about
39,000	to over 60,000, or about 50 per cent. What can one say about the armed forces? The most significant observation about our armed forces is their relative numerical weakness in the lower ranks and their top-heavy nature. Their personnel includes only 19,300 privates, or merely 25 per cent of total military personnel, some 43,000 non-commissioned officers, and more than 14,000 officers. There are nearly twice as many captains as lieutenants, and nearly 50 per cent more corporals than privates.
I bring these facts forward to counter the government's argument that when the older spouse dies it must, because of the cost factor, take away the allowance from the surviving
Old Age Security
spouse if that spouse has not reached age 65. That is inequitable and 1 resent the government's suggestion that we on my side of the House are urging the government to spend more money. That is a fallacious argument. The fact is that almost any department of government one cares to examine wastes more money than it would cost to provide this program which has as its basis a humanitarian concern. Surely the government cannot say that it cannot afford the program, for it would cost only $700,000. To repeat what my former leader said, this government wastes more money than it would need to provide the spouses' program. The money would be only a little dribble. It should provide these funds to spouses who are without them. That is all I can say.
I underscore this: the arguments made by members on the government side yesterday were invalid and perhaps even designed to mislead the House. It was suggested that the program would cost an additional $2 billion. By the minister's own admission in committee, the cost would not be nearly as great. That point needs to be made.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to participate in this debate until I heard some hon. members speaking yesterday. I was inspired to enter the debate by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and also prompted by a personal experience on Tuesday night of this week. I shall deal with the second reason immediately. I was attending a meeting of the ward 8 ratepayers' association in my riding to discuss the question of railway crossings when the president announced the death of one of the members of the association. Another member was collecting money to assist the widow. The question arose, why were people collecting money for the widow? The answer was that the husband who had passed on was over 65 years old and his wife, under 65, had been getting the spouse's allowance. Now, because the husband had passed on, the widow was to get nothing.

speechtext:
Yes, people at the meeting were collecting money to assist the widow.
When we debated the spouses' allowance a couple of years ago we were told that the amendment before the House was based on the theory that two pensioners could not live on one pension. Hence the reason for the spouses' allowance. I remember that all opposition members who spoke tried to persuade the government not to include in the amendment the exceptions affecting widows, widowers, spinsters and bachelors. All people in the age range of 60 to 65 should be given an allowance, especially if the pensioner has passed on. I heard the response yesterday by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) about persons on spouses' allowance who, as a result of the death of a person receiving the pension, will get nothing. It made me realize that I had to get up and say something, especially when I had the personal experience I mentioned on Tuesday night.

What did the Minister of National Health and Welfare say? He said that to pay a pension to people between 60 and 65 years of age would cost $2 billion and that we in the opposition ought to exercise some financial responsibility. The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) said it is very easy for the opposition to talk about changes in programs, but these improvements have to be made by increased taxes. He said it is not realistic to make these changes at the moment. The hon. member decried the members of the Conservative party who he claims have stated they want it both ways. He said they want government restraint on one side, and at the same time they want improvements in programs. I thought the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone) ably set forth the argument with regard to the amount of money the government is spending on other programs and the necessity of having priorities with regard to its expenditures. When one thinks of the $25 million loss on the sale of the CANDU reactor to Argentina, one realizes that the government has not set its priorities in order. When one considers the corporate advantages with regard to depreciation allowances, and the huge savings to corporations as a result of those tax advantages, one realizes that the government does not have its priorities in order.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare said it would cost $2 billion to pay pensions to persons aged 60 to 65. He does not realize the real thrust of the argument of members of the Conservative party, the New Democratic Party and, I am sure, the Social Credit party with regard to spouses' allowances. In reality, the cost of the program to permit spouses' allowances to continue until they attain 65 years of age, on the minister's own admission in committee, amounts to $700,000. Now, $700,000 is a far different figure from the $2 billion that the minister gave. It was a deliberate attempt to mislead the House with regard to this matter.
I am rather happy that the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) is in the chamber. I hope she participates in the debate. The real thrust of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in bringing forth the motion to refer back to committee clauses 8 and 9 of Bill C-35 was to persuade the government that this should be done and that they should accept the pleadings and arguments made in committee by the hon. member for York South-and made many times from this side of the House-that the spouses' allowance should stand regardless of age until the person attains 65 years of age. This gives the hon. member for York South, the hon. member for Davenport and hon. members on the opposite side an opportunity to tell the Minister of National Health and Welfare in no uncertain terms that there is a deliberate injustice to these people by cutting them off the spouses' allowance because one member of the relationship passes on. I hope the hon. member for York South participates in the debate and in the vote to give us support to have this matter referred back to committee.
Why is it that the Liberal party always casts shadows on good programs and principles? I remind hon. members of the

label they earned, and deserved, back in 1957 when they attempted to give pensioners a $6 increase. They were known as the "six-buck boys". The result of that action was that they lost the next election to the Conservative party. I recall two or three years ago when at Christmas the government, in an endeavour to adjust the old age pension, gave old age pensioners a 42-cent increase. Why is it that two years ago they made those cruel and inhumane amendments with regard to the spouses' allowance affecting widows, widowers, bachelors and spinsters?
I ask the hon. member for York South and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), why it is that the Liberal party casts a shadow on programs that are essentially good? Why is it they get so mean, miserable and niggardly with regard to certain people within the community? This is why we in the New Democratic Party think the motion presented by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre gives all of us an opportunity to tell the government in no uncertain terms that this is not the way most Canadians want to treat widows, widowers, bachelors and spinsters with regard to pensions.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has a very high-profile portfolio. However, he was disappointing when he attempted to justify his action by the statements he made yesterday. I spoke about the widow in my constituency who will be cut off her spouses' allowance because her husband passed on. She gets nothing. The minister had the audacity to say that she can apply for social assistance or welfare. There is a difference between a pension and welfare assistance. A pension is earned. Welfare assistance appears to be a grant or gift, something that may not be earned. Surely the wives and husbands of pensioners who are under 65 years of age should be treated in a more humane way.
When I heard the response of the minister that we have to tackle the problem of poverty, I could not agree with him more. However, I say to him that it is about time he started tackling the problem of poverty. It was not enough for the Minister of National Health and Welfare to go to Toronto last Friday and attempt to lecture the people of Toronto and Ontario by saying they must put their actions where their words are with regard to national unity. It was not enough for him to say they have to take the initiative with regard to programs in language, attitudes, and so forth. He has to tackle the problem in a more concrete and specific manner.
The minister would have been far better to go to Toronto and say to the people of Ontario that if we want national unity we have to tackle the problems of poverty, unemployment, housing and many of the social problems that prevail. If he had done that, instead of trying to lecture them on the bilingual issue, I am sure that he would have obtained the support of the people of Ontario, indeed of people throughout Canada. It is not worthy of a minister in a high-profile portfolio to say that sort of thing.
March 10, 1977

1 would remind the minister that one thing we have to get straight is basic security for all Canadians. I give the government credit for the Canada Pension Plan, but we have to be reminded at all times that at best the Canada pension provides only 25 per cent of the six best years of a workingman's life, which 1 suggest is not sufficient to meet today's costs. In view of the high rate of inflation today, is it any wonder that people who receive the Canada pension have to continue working to meet the expenses of the day?
At this stage, Mr.' Speaker, it is only right and proper that all of us should give full credit to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre who has spoken on pensions ever since he came into the House and yesterday put the position on pensions clearly and concisely. Many members, including the hon. member for Davenport, picked up points which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre made, as did the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), not only with regard to spouses' allowance but also with regard to the double signature required on some pension application forms. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre also outlined the problem faced 10 or 12 years down the road by people who come to Canada today and who, as a result of the changes contained in Bill C-35, may not have sufficient money to meet requirements of that day.
I was rather amused at the performance of the hon. member for Hamilton West yesterday, who jumped up after the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had moved his motion to refer back clauses 8 and 9 of the bill to test the strength of the opposition regarding spouses' allowance and said that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had not told him what he was attempting to do. Mr. Speaker, there has always been a rather pleasant relationship between members of the New Democratic Party and members of the Conservative party concerning opposition we have to government programs, but this is the first time I have known a member to jump up and criticize our critic because he had not told him what he was going to do. I just could not get over the fact that he would whine and try to say that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was devious. I think he should have thanked the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and said that he appreciated the opportunity given to him procedurally to express his concern about pensioners.

I think at this stage in our so-called civilization the one thing we cannot afford to do is to overlook the human factor. I happen to believe that as legislators, as human beings, it is our duty to uphold each one's dignity and to save each one's pride. There is a sentiment, especially among our elderly, that hand-outs in the form of welfare, or whatever euphemism you care to use, are beneath their dignity. We might quarrel with, dispute and question the rationale behind that sentiment, but we cannot dispute the fact that the sentiment exists and that somehow we have to uphold the dignity of these people to whom this situation is very real. For some reason it is much more important to them to accept a cheque from the federal government than it is to accept one from the welfare office of a province or municipality. That cannot be disputed and must be accepted.

March 10, 1977
Old Age Security
Now let me take the case of widows and widowers aged 60 and over. They suddenly lose their spouse. They are by age and by every other concept in our language at the most vulnerable point of their lives. What are we doing to them? We are taking a few pennies away. Let us face it, we are not giving them through OAS a tremendous amount of money, but we are taking away the few pennies that their dignity demands, and doing this at the very time they have lost their loved ones. Is that humanity?
I have dealt with widows and widowers. What are we doing with the unwed? We have allowed common law marriage, but this is not the question here. What, in effect, this bill is doing is penalizing or victimizing those people who for one reason or another chose not to marry.
Let me quote just one case in point. We have a man aged 65 or over who for one reason-mainly cultural, I might add-is given the usual comforts of life. He is cooked for, he is cared for in many ways by his sister who is over 60. Obviously, they cannot marry. They do not want to be spouses unless they want an incestuous relationship. Perhaps I had better keep away from that. But just because they are not married, this sister who has given him all the comforts he needs in his old age is denied anything. The rationale behind this, we are told, is that two people cannot live on one pension. What happens to the sister who does not marry? She is excluded. In other words, we are penalizing the woman. It is usually the woman. I am sorry if I sound feminist-no, I am not sorry; I do not apologize: it is usually the women who are penalized.

speechtext: You are right.

I regret my error in 1975 and want to rectify it now. I want the government to show its humanity.

It is, indeed, a pity that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) was not present to hear those comments. 1 sincerely hope they will be passed on to him quickly, before the vote, and that they will have an influence on the way in which he reacts to the amendment. I should like to comment on the amendment put forward by the

hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, my party has expressed its intention to support Bill C-35. But what we are debating at the moment is an amendment which I feel would improve the bill and at the same time remove a particularly cruel form of injustice which presently exists.
The origin of that injustice goes back to Bill C-62 of last session, a bill debated in the spring of 1975. I state again, as I did at that time, that certain provisions of Bill C-62 were conceived in a spirit of meanness and callousness. That piece of legislation enabled the younger spouse of an old age pensioner to receive old age security, on the basis of need, between 60 and 65 years of age. A number of us who served on the committee of that time, all members of opposition parties, felt the benefits of such a proposal should not be denied to those who had the misfortune to lose the elder partner in a marriage, or to single persons in the same age category.
We were particularly incensed that a younger spouse who became the recipient of the payment on a regular basis should suddently have that payment terminated on the death of the elder partner. This seemed to us to be cruel, unjust and unfair. We protested strongly at the time. The amendment before us, introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, seeks to redress that callous action on the part of the government.
Statistics show that in 90 per cent of all marital union, the younger spouse is female and, as in so many other areas of discrimination, the inequity falls far more heavily on women than on men. It is ironic that this particular inequity should have been initiated by the minister responsible for the status of women.

speechtext: Shame.

speechtext:
I recall that back in June, 1975, the minister was asked whether any projection had been made as to the number of people who would become disentitled to pensions on the death of the elder spouse. The minister asked his officials for the projection, and the figures indicated that some 375 persons per month would be disentitled; that is, approximately 4,500 Canadians per year. So the figure is
4.500	people out of a total population of some 23 million. Not a great number, but obviously too few to warrant the concern of the government.
What does it mean in dollar terms? If you take the figure of
4.500	a year and calculate on the basis of the maximum benefit rate of $150 a month-and many people would not be receiving as much as that-the total amount would come to about $672,000 a year which, as some members have already pointed out, is less than the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) spends annually on his private jet flights. If you were to take another figure, that is, the $40 million which the government lost and pilfered away on the sale of the CANDU reactor to Argentina, and transfer it to those 4,500 people who are disentitled annually, you would be able to continue paying pensions to people in this category for the next 50 years.

I want the minister to tell us if he knows what a person feels like when suddently cut off from benefits. Has he ever been in contact with such individuals? Has he ever listened to them? Has he ever talked to them? If so, what does he tell them about this? Yesterday, when he was addressing himself to the amendment, he proudly trumpeted these words: "We have no lesson to learn from anybody." As was said of the Bourbons, so it could be said of the Minister of National Health and Welfare: he has learned nothing and he has forgotten nothing.
I suggest the minister learn to listen to a few of these people to whom he is causing such unnecessary hardship. It may be trite to say the government is practicing restraint upon the backs of the poor and the aged, but that is certainly what is being done in this case.
In his usual devious manner, the minister sought to distort the amendment by claiming that its intent would cost some $2 billion. Obviously, his figure is inaccurate if you look at that amendment and, I would say, deliberately inaccurate. But if there is one thing that we have learned to expect from this government, it is that it is pretty poor at doing its arithmetic on anything. Some 4,500 Canadians are affected annually by this discriminatory piece of legislation-4,500 Canadians who have already had to prove their need in order to receive this payment. I suggest that if there was need in the first place for them to receive payment, surely that need exists to a greater, not a lesser, degree after the death of the older spouse. I want to see these benefits retained by the 4,500 Canadians who are presently receiving them. The minister wants to snatch them back, and again I have no doubt that he will vote against the amendment: he said he would do so.
He also said something else back in 1975 when he was before the committee. He told the members at that time that he would provide us with a copy of the letter of notification which he sends bereaved pensioners notifying them that they are no longer eligible for benefits. Perhaps now is the time for him to do so; now is the time for him to make that letter public when he takes this uncharitable action today in voting against this amendment, because his uncharitable letter of disentitle-ment would certainly be a suitable accompanying gesture to that action.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Parry-Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling) says that I am kind of harsh on Bell. I am not. I was prepared to let the goodness of my heart overflow in dealing with this bill, but when I saw the text yesterday in the Globe and Mail of the president of Bell, Mr. James Thackray, that was it-my goodness blew away. I want to quote from the testimony of Mr. Thackray before the CRTC yesterday regarding Bell's latest application for a rate increase. According to the Globe and Mail:
Bell Canada may stop installing new telephones service if the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission does not give it the full rate increase it wants, according to Bell president James Thackray.
There is a threat which one of Canada's multinationals and largest companies has thrown out to the regulatory body set up to regulate Bell Canada's rate increases. When I read that I became very interested and wanted to participate in this debate to the full. In digging around for material I discovered some rather interesting things about this particular bill. When it was brought to this House several weeks ago and my colleague for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) spoke on this bill, he clearly indicated that the thrust of the bill is to increase the capitalization of Bell Canada without reference to the regulatory body, the CRTC.
So here we have a corporation which is regulated because at the time of the setting up of the body to govern this corporation it was seen that the corporation ought to act in the best interests of Canada and Canadians. One would assume that a lot of corporations try to maximize profits, but the thrust of this bill appears to be to minimize regulations so there is no reference back to the House whatsoever, and this concerns us.
The first thing that threw me off about this bill, Mr. Speaker, is that it originated in the other place. If there is one thing in this House which makes me very skeptical and run immediately to the record, it is to see what those minions of the corporate sector in that last bastion of capitalist free enterprise in this country have to say about a bill. No one looking at the list of senators in the other place would doubt that they are indeed experts in the way the economy works and in the way financial institutions work. So I said to myself, "Now, fellow, you had better get the debates of the Senate committee and the debates of the Senate and read what they have to say, because I am sure there will be words of wisdom for any member". So that is what I did, Mr. Speaker. I had a little bit of difficulty because it took this bill one day, exactly, to go through committee stage and third reading debate, occupying one page of Senate Hansard. But I want to tell the House that those gems of wisdom that I was looking for were missing. There was not one expose of why Bell Canada wanted this legislation.
Before the Senate committee meeting, which I presume all took place in the space of an hour or so, was Mr. A. J. de Grandpre, chairman and chief executive officer of Bell
March 10, 1977

Canada. It appears he was the only one who spoke throughout the brief committee meeting on December 14, 1976. Some senators may have said, "Phew, it is warm in here; can we open a window?", but there was no questioning of Mr. de Grandpre. Interestingly enough, he gave a very abbreviated history of Bell Canada and he had this gem of a statement, to be found at page 1:7 of the Senate Standing Committee on Transport and Communications report:
Bell Canada is a typical example of a company which was, at one time, under American control and influence and which has been gradually brought back into Canadian hands, not by decree or legislation, but by long-term planning and performance.
Well, Mr. Speaker, since we have had Mr. de Grandpre's abbreviated history of the development of Bell, I think it only fair to this House that I put on record a more complete and detailed history of the development of Bell Canada. I think it is important to take a look at the development of Bell because, in effect, we will see certain practices of and developments in Bell which we should look at in light of today's threats which were made before the CRTC by Mr. Thackray, in light of the manner in which Bell wants to develop, in light of some of their responses to the need for rural service, in light of the propaganda they put out, and in light of their political influence in the other place and even in this House. This is why I want to put the real history of Bell Canada on the record. It will then be there for generations of Canadians to read and to get the other side of the picture.
Alexander Graham Bell obtained the basic patent on the telephone for the United States on March 7, 1876, and a second patent on January 30, 1877. These two patents formed the basis of the Bell system monopoly in the United States until their expiration in 1893 and 1894. Recognizing the competitive potential of the telephone upon telegraph service, however, the Western Union Telegraph Company attempted to enter the telephone business on the basis of competing patents held by Elisha Gray, Thomas Edison, and others, in 1878.
The Western Union Telegraph Company and the American Speaking Telephone Company in 1879 signed an agreement with Bell Telephone Company, a predecessor of I.T. & T., which admitted to the validity of the Bell patents. It agreed to withdraw from the telephone field, and in exchange Western Union was to receive 20 per cent of all rentals or royalties received by the Bell Company from telephone instruments for a period of 17 years and Bell was not to enter the telegraph field.
Canadian patents for the telephone were given by Alexander Graham Bell to his father Alexander Melville Bell for $1 and to Charles Williams of Boston for 1,000 telephone instruments. Melville Bell hired agents to solicit subscribers for private lines in Canada, and in 1879 the Dominion Telegraph Company became the general agent for the Bell interests in Canada. It secured a licence to operate Bell patents for five years. However, the Dominion Telegraph Company found it impossible to raise the $100,000 demanded by Melville Bell for
Bell Canada
the purchase of the patents and later that year the Canadian patent rights were sold to associates of the National Bell Telephone Company of Boston. This group brought Charles Fleetford Sise to Canada to organize the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
Rival telephone service was offered by the Montreal Telegraph Company, an affiliate of Western Union, utilizing the Edison patents. For a time, both telegraph companies offered telephone services in Montreal. In other communities, telephone service was offered by local groups under the arrangements with Melville Bell prior to the agreement between Bell and the Dominion Telegraph Company. For example, in Hamilton telephone service was offered by the Hamilton District Telegraph Company in 1878, later the Hamilton Telephone Company which opened the first telephone exchange in Canada.
In 1880, two subsidiaries of the National Bell Telephone Company in the United States were incorporated under federal charter. The Bell Telephone Company of Canada was incorporated in 1880 and given certain powers. Those powers were outlined in the course of the proceedings of the select committee on telephones. They were as follows:
-to manufacture telephones and other apparatus connected therewith used in connection with the business of a telegraph or a telephone company, and to purchase, sell or lease the same and rights relating thereto, and to build, establish, construct, purchase, acquire or lease, and maintain and operate, or sell or let any line or lines for the transmission of messages by telephone in Canada or elsewhere.
The company was empowered to construct and maintain its telephone lines along the sides of and across or under any public highways, streets, bridges, water courses and other such places. Attempts were made by legislators to submit the new company to regulation of tolls through the provisions of the 1875 telegraph act, but they were defeated. We should note, at this point, a voice from history coming to us over time. A solemn warning was sounded at that time. A member of the other place, Senator Haythorne, called attention to the danger which might arise and he did so at the time the Telegraph Act was implemented. This is what he said, and I quote from the debates of the Senate:
There is nothing which this House ought to look after with greater jealousy than the establishment of large monopolies ... I consider it one of my most important duties as a legislator to guard against the evils of monopolies.
That was a warning which has obviously not been heeded over the years. It is one we should keep in mind as we debate Bill S-2. Under various agreements in 1880, Bell Canada obtained exclusive patent rights to offer telephone service in this country. The Canadian telephone company was set up as a subsidiary of Bell (United States) to hold the patent rights and to own all telephone instruments in Canada. The Bell Telephone Company of Canada was incorporated to lease the patent rights and to lease telephone instruments from that company. In 1884 and 1885 the Canadian patent rights held by Bell Canada were voided by the minister of agriculture on the grounds of non-manufacture and refusal to sell. This opened the way for the establishment of independent telephone
3858

March 10, 1977
Bell Canada
companies, provided they could secure easements and rights-of-way.
Due to high rates, refusal to extend service and poor technical standards on the part of Bell, a large number of telephone companies arose, many of them in direct competition with Bell. In reaction to this Bell lowered the price for telephone service, sometimes to zero, when faced by direct competition. In his testimony before the select committee on telephones, here is what Mr. Sise had to say, and I quote his evidence:
There was a time in Peterborough when we charged nothing for our service and your argument (on discrimination) would be that we would have to give a free service all over Canada.
One of the committee members then commented:
In Peterborough, you gave it to them for nothing. That is very cheap.
To which the witness replied:
I do not know that anybody in Peterborough ever objected.
Well, they were loss-leadering telephones in those days. It was one of their ways of destroying competition. When I see the advertisement, "Let's free enterprise", when I hear corporate leaders telling government that it should not interfere in the operations of legitimate business, I confess I am irritated because when we look at history we find that the principle upon which business has operated has been one of eliminating competition, not of encouraging it. Here we find Bell Telephone engaged in loss-leadering to eliminate competition. Then this gentleman, Mr. Sise, stood up and said, "Yes, we did it", and nobody complained.
As I say, Bell's policy involved, first of all, predatory pricing. Second, it involved refusal to interconnect services. Bell refused to interconnect competing companies with its telephone exchange, thereby barring such companies from access to its long distance facilities. The third aspect of this policy was that of collusion with the railway companies. Bell succeeded in preventing independent companies from gaining access to railway stations by offering the railways free telephone service in exchange for this exclusive privilege. Finally, there was the aspect of propaganda. Bell paid newspapers to publish false and misleading allegations regarding its competitors.
The one example which stands out in my mind is the situation involving the muncipalities of Port Arthur and Fort William in northern Ontario. These two towns had established a municipal telephone system. Incidentally, it is still in existence today. In 1902 both towns agreed, due to the discontent over the service provided by Bell during the preceding five years, to set up a joint system with provision for the exchange of conversations. To indicate the degree of discontent with the Bell service, I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that only 15 persons among all those to whom a plebiscite was sent voted against the construction of a municipally-owned system. The municipal systems commenced operations in November, 1902, and in March, 1903, one of the exchanges was sabotaged and burned mysteriously. As a matter of fact, the evidence given by the mayor of Fort William, Joshua Dyke, to the select committee

on telephone which was investigating the situation reads as follows:
One still, drizzly night.. . about two in the morning someone connected the 2,000 volt electric wires to the 30 volt telephone wires, thereby destroying the exchange. During the time in which the municipal system-

Mr. Speaker, I am rather disappointed in some of the Liberal members not allowing the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) to continue relating a very interesting and exciting incident concerning the Bell Telephone Company. I will continue the story if I have time at the end of my remarks, but first I have some important things to say with regard to Bill S-2.
I should like to start by saying that I have been here 11 years, and in that time I have seen the erosion of the public accountability of many corporations operating in Canada. There are two types of corporation, the private corporation and the public corporation. When I came here, most private corporations were under the control and regulations of the Canada Corporations Act. There are certain corporations which have to be regulated, controlled and incorporated by the federal government, such as banks, insurance companies and some trust companies. Before they could get letters patent of incorporation, their capitalization, their objects and purposes and many other factors were scrutinized by parliament.
In my 11 years here I have seen a gradual erosion in some of these institutions. Banks can now operate under the Canada Corporations Act and are no longer under the scrutiny of parliament. Insurance companies are treated in the same way. In fact, very few public corporations which now operate right across the country are scrutinized by parliament to determine whether they should be given letters patent to operate and whether they should be allowed amendments to their letters patent. Bill S-2 is a typical example of that. It is an attempt by a corporation which is privately owned and which issues public shares to free itself of the control of parliament. Therefore, it is a very important bill because it affects social and public accountability.
I was rather impressed by the historical and factual background of Bell Canada which the hon. member for Nickel Belt gave. We see that the company originated in the United States and developed in Canada. He traced very convincingly and with great clarity the manner in which that company has operated since its inception in Canada. It has had a tremendous effect on Canadians. In fact, most Canadians feel rather sentimental and affectionate with regard to the Bell Telephone Company which they sometimes call Ma Bell. Ma Bell needs to be checked and scrutinized, and we in the NDP feel it is
March 10, 1977

incumbent upon us, when the company brings forth amendments to their letters patent, not to permit them to do things which will free them from the control of parliament over their conduct and operations.
I heard the hon. member for Nickel Belt say that the president of Bell Telephone appeared before the CRTC and said that if the company did not receive rate increases it would stop installing telephones across the country. Let me point out that this is not new for Bell Telephone. They had threatened it in certain parts of Ontario, especially in the Bramalea area where there was a new housing development in which people needed telephones. It was only as a result of public pressure that the Bell Telephone Company yielded and installed telephones. In the last six years there have been no less than five or six applications by Bell Telephone Company to increase their rates. This brings into perspective the need to study the purposes and objectives of the Bell Telephone Company because we feel a telephone company operating in telecommunications should be a public utility servicing Canadians at the lowest cost possible.
That is what we in the NDP believe, namely, that the Bell Telephone Company should be a public utility operated for the benefit of all Canadians at the lowest possible cost. Recently I saw some Bell Telephone advertisements on television which I found to be clever, expensive and, in many cases, immoral as one of my colleagues has said because a public utility should provide a service as its first objective and should seek to be profitable as its second objective. Therefore, the costs should be minimal. This is what we in the NDP are saying.
Having set forth that main proposition, I notice that the mover of the motion, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell), who is an economist by profession, is listening attentively to what I am saying because he knows that under the present system we operate on a profit basis. However, we say that the profit objective of a public utility should be secondary, not primary. We know that there are two types of costs, capital costs and current costs. Capital costs are absolutely necessary for further expansion, yet we all know that sophisticated equipment is necessary to give better service to subscribers. Not one member of the NDP would challenge the expenditure of capital costs provided they were reasonable, because we realize that by providing capital costs we may obtain, through sophisticated equipment, the best possible service. There are also costs which take into account wages and other ordinary operating expenses. Again we feel that the working-man should be given a reasonable wage for the service he performs. We have no objection to a reasonable wage for Bell Telephone workers. In fact we have stood on the front line to assist workers across the country to receive a decent and fair wage.
There should be a reasonable profit concept. Any profit should be reasonable. It should be up to the representatives in parliament to study in detail what Bell Telephone means by a reasonable profit concept. We in parliament have said that we
Bell Canada
would like to set up a regulatory body to study in detail the movements and approaches of the Bell Telephone Company with regard to its profits. I said in my earlier remarks that the Bell Telephone Company has made an application for a rate increase every year for the last five or six years. Therefore it behooves all of us to determine whether Bell is making a reasonable profit.
It is absolutely necessary to have a regulatory body such as CRTC to determine Bell's rates and for parliament to set out the telecommunications philosophy. That philosophy may be that there should be public ownership, that there should be private ownership, or that there should be part public ownership and part private ownership, but from my casual study of the profits of Bell I think I am being very gentle when I say that it is a carnivorous corporate giant. It makes unregulated profits which are not reviewed by the CRTC. It has been said many times that the widows of Canada purchase shares in the Bell Telephone Company so that they can make a profit, be paid dividends, and enhance their security. Many of us feel compassion toward widows when it comes to the matter of security, but we do not think that Bell Telephone is the vehicle by which they should get their security. The basic thrust of the Bell Telephone Company should be service to a certain segment, and people should come before profits.
Over the last month I have had the opportunity to read a book about International Telephone and Telegraph, which is a large corporate organization operating in the United States. It also operates in Europe and in Chile, and when we look at International Telephone and Telegraph's multinational operations we find that it has no less than 400 corporations under its wing. I have the very uneasy feeling that Bell Canada may want to operate in the same way as International Telephone and Telegraph. When I know of the political intrusion in Chile of Harold Geneen, who is the president of ITT, and when I know of his financial support of the overthrow of a democratically-elected government, I feel it is my responsibility to check and double check any utility in Canada which wants to take itself out from under the regulatory powers of CRTC and beyond the scrutiny of parliament.
Those are general remarks, and I would now like to make some specific remarks about Bill S-2 because we are studying the philosophy and principle of the bill and some of its provisions. As the hon. member for Nickel Belt said, it is odd that this type of bill should be initiated in the other place. It shocks me to be advised that it took less than a day to pass it in the other place. It shocks me that a bill of such magnitude and of such importance should be considered in less than a day and that only one witness should appear before the committee. That witness was the chairman of the board, who attempted to give a very brief history of the company. That very same person threatened Canadians that if there is a separation of Quebec, Bell may move its head office from Quebec. If we are talking about national unity, it behooves the chairman, Mr. de Grandpre, not to make that kind of statement with regard to the operations of Bell in Quebec.
80010-38%

March 10, 1977
Bell Canada
We must remember that only 7 per cent of all Bell's revenue comes from competitive operations and that 93 per cent of its profits comes from telephone services. There should be public accountability, and telephone and telecommunications operations in Canada should be treated as a public utility rather than as a corporation operating for the purpose of earning profits for shareholders.
Bill S-2 proposes two distinct amendments to Bell's act of incorporation. It proposes the revision of the act of incorporation relating to the company's ability and methodology of capitalization, including the removal of the scrutiny of the appropriate government regulatory body, namely, the CRTC.
The bill grants Bell the power to borrow, issue stock, bonds, debentures or other securities as the company deems necessary. In addition, the bill would give Bell the right to fix whatever price on such sales as it wishes. It is a necessity to have a telephone company operate for the people at a reasonable cost. Bell enjoys a monopoly. It wants to bypass parliament and the CRTC. It wants power to borrow, issue stocks, bonds, debentures and other securities, and to fix whatever price on sales it wishes.
Subsequent clauses would provide Bell with the authority to establish such voting rights, by-laws, procedures and alterations to share issues as Bell may deem necessary. The present authorized capital of the company is $1.75 billion. Bell proposes to increase its capitalization capacity to $5 billion. That would be an increase of three times its present authorized capital.
I note that the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Elaidasz) is listening attentively. He realizes the importance of the increase in capitalization, the changes in the capital structure and the voting structure, the changes in the borrowing powers and so forth.
The second amendment proposes broadening the company's incidental and ancillary powers, and proposes that the company be given the authority for the alteration by letters patent of the company's objectives and powers. That is very important because once we start dealing with the company's objectives and powers, we are talking about the company's total operations. At the moment it has a monopoly of telephone service and telecommunications services in some instances. Once the objects of the company are changed, however, it would mean it could not only increase its vertical operations but also its horizontal operations. It could get into the money business in the same way that ITT in the United States has done.
ITT has more than 400 companies under its wing-it is almost a nation in itself-and it dictates the rates, makes the highest possible profits, and sometimes resorts to unwarranted political interference. This would be achieved by revoking the relevant clauses in Bell's act of incorporation and replacing them with the authority granted under the Canada Corporations Act and authority for using letters patent as outlined in the Telesat Canada Act. Proposed section 5.2 and 5.3 of clause 2 in Bill S-2 are the essential elements of this objective.

Mr. Speaker, the last time a bill relating to Bell Canada came before the House of Commons was just a few years ago. As far as I am concerned it would be here still if it had been possible to arrange that. I was very concerned then, as I am now, with the question of whether Bell Canada is serving the public or is bilking the public for the benefit of the shareholders or someone else in the corporation. At that time it was simply asking to add five members to the board of directors. I was able to propose an amendment suggesting that one of those directors be appointed by the government without the requirements normally stipulated, that he hold a certain amount of stock, and other considerations and that such a person have the function of protecting the public. Of course, Bell made a great fuss. I did not suggest who the government should name to the board; the important thing was that the appointee be there to protect the general subscriber.
Bell Canada is not like any other company, but its lines run down the road, run down the street, run down the lane in exactly the same way as hydro lines. There can only be one telephone company in a town. Even people who believe that free enterprise must triumph at the expense of the public would agree that there cannot be four or five telephone companies in the same town. Bell got rid of other companies in the country, but even Bell would not suggest there could be competition in a community. So the company has a monopoly. It is operated to supply a service to the people, but the free enterprisers allowed it to do something else, to be established as a private company and at the same time gain a considerable return on its money. It was set up to provide the service and make money for its shareholders.
Over the years the company has made application to parliament when it wanted to change its relationship with the shareholders or wanted to change its rate structure. We have not been hard on this company, Mr. Speaker. It is a big company and enjoys quite a reputation in the country. This is a very lenient country and has allowed this public utility to expand beyond the boundaries of Canada. It is interesting to note how much money it has made in the process. It has not made money any way except by subterfuge in the market or by selling something, whether it be expertise or service.
I am not interested particularly in its subterfuge in the business world, but I am interested in what happens to the subscriber. Because I consider this to be a public utility I would be happy to join with members of this House, who should be working on behalf of the people, to see that a proper service is provided to subscribers at the lowest possible cost.
March 10, 1977

If necessary, I would support a move to nationalize this public utility. I would not care too much about whether we sold all the subsidiaries, although it seems to me we are treating them as we are the CPR, that is, giving away a very large grant.
The list of subsidiaries in which Bell owns more than 50 per cent of outstanding shares is interesting. Here is a breakdown: Northern Telcom Ltd., 69.2 per cent; Bell Northern Research, Ltd., 51 per cent; the New Brunswick Telephone Company, 50.4 per cent; Newfoundland Telephone Company, Ltd., 78.2 per cent; Northern Telephone, Ltd., 99.7 per cent; Telebec Ltee, 95.1 per cent; Liviere Valley Telephone Company, 100 per cent; Capital Telephone Company, Ltd., 100 per cent; TelOntario Incorporated, 100 per cent; the North American Telegraph Company, 100 per cent; and Maritime Telegraph and Telephone Company, Ltd., 51.7 per cent. I should like to refer particularly to a couple of these subsidiaries. Every cent of the money that bought them came from the shareholders or the subscribers. Bell has been set up as a corporation that has shareholders, and it should be pointed out how it has taken advantage of them. If we agree to this application then we agree to watering down the stock.
Bell Canada owns the Capital Telephone Company, Ltd., just a litte company not far from the city of Ottawa that was formely owned by the subscribers. There was an exchange at Carp, one at Constance Bay, and one at Maberly serving 2,031 telephones. This was bought with the subscribers' money; we are not really going to believe that the shareholders put up the money. They really did not know what was happening, and in some cases it was not happening for the shareholder but to the shareholder. This was certainly true in some of the subsidiary companies.
Bell wanted to do a number of things. It wanted to produce telephone books. Consequently, Tele-Direct was set up. Mr. Speaker, Tele-Direct is an example of Bell's ability to spin-off profitable sectors of operations to subsidiaries, to escape regulation. At the same time that sort of move enhances Bell's rate case when applying for rate increases. Therefore, Bell takes money out of the operation, which provides a good excuse for asking for another increase.
Until 1971 Bell produced its own directories. That was and still is a most lucrative proposition, because those directories carry advertising. If anything, the operation has become even more lucrative. Now the printing in the directories is so small that you have to pay somebody 25 cents to find a telephone number.

In 1969, revenue was $35 million, and net revenue before tax $15.5 million.
To escape regulation, Bell sold this sector of its operation, Tele-Direct, to Capital Telephone Company, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bell. Mr. Speaker, since Capital has always
Bell Canada
operated in the province of Ontario and has no exchanges outside the province, it is regulated by the province of Ontario.
We never worry about these companies until they ask for a rate increase. Once they ask for a rate increase, you start making inquiries. What did Bell do with regard to Capital's exchanges? It took over two of the exchanges, but left alone one little exchange at Maberly which serves 121 telephones. If you live in Maberly your telephone rate will never go up. No matter if Bell rates to other subscribers rise to $50 a month, rates to Maberly subscribers will stay at the level of the take-over in 1969. Why will they stay at that level? Bell is not giving away something for nothing.
Bell is able to do some remarkable things with this little company-and this information is available from CRTC experts. Bell owned Tele-Direct, which it sold to Capital, and Tele-Direct controls Place Bell Canada, that showcase of Bell Canada. No one will say that 121 subscribers support a company big enough to put out telephone directories, own printing plants, and all the rest of it. But the small company can rent Place Bell Canada back to the large telephone company. It then becomes an expense to the telephone company.
It may interest those from the Maritimes to know that Capital Telephone owns a fleet of fishing trawlers.

speechtext: Are you speaking about a telephone company?

A telephone company, yes. Also, I am told it owns Bell executive jets, and rents them back to the company, always at great cost to Bell.
Nobody is ever going to look at Capital Telephone, Mr. Speaker. There will never be an occasion when Capital Telephone will approach the Ontario government and say, "We want our subscribers to pay increased rates." Talk about a rate increase! They are having one hell of a time getting rid of the money they earn.
According to my latest figures, the book cost of Capital Telephone was $1.2 million in 1969; by 1974 the book cost had risen to $4.2 million. And how much income do you suppose 121 subscribers generated? Why, the company's total income in 1974 was $3 million. Bell's share of that net income amounted to $3 million. The little company's earnings sure did not help its subscribers. They were not compensated for having telephones in their houses. If they all took their telephones out, there would be no justification for Capital's existence. It is interesting to note that Bell's return on the book cost of Capital Telephone was, in 1974, $64.3 million. Did they raise that from 121 subscribers? Let's not kid ourselves. Telephone companies don't make that much money, unless they are not telephone companies but something else.
In our consideration of this bill, we are not talking about allowing Bell to increase its capitalization from $1.7 billion to $5 billion. We are not talking about the raising of capital for the development of a telephone company.

Then what are we talking about?

I mentioned some of Bell's subsidiary companies. Bell already owns a 27 per cent share of Telesat, that satellite in the sky. What will the company do with all the money it wants?
