subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration) moved
subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
that Bill C-24, respecting immigration to Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I sometimes wonder how the minister felt some 25 years ago when he stood on second reading of the 1952 bill. I am sure that he thought it historic. 1 want to say for future generations I feel this is in fact an historic moment because it is in the final analysis the coming together of a tremendous amount of work by many thousands of Canadians. I hope we have been able to incorporate into this bill that which will be to the betterment of Canada and be of benefit to future generations.
I am sure that all members know that the genesis of this bill dates from an announcement made by my predecessor, now the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), just over three years ago. On September 17, 1973, he informed the House that the government was launching a fundamental review of immigration policy in the widest possible context as a first step toward the preparation of modern legislation on which to base the future conduct of Canada's immigration program.
The process that undertaking set in motion has involved an unprecedented nation-wide debate. Literally thousands of organizations and individuals across the country responded to the government's invitation to submit briefs. Conferences and seminars were organized, many with the financial support of my department. Throughout the entire period, provincial governments have been closely consulted.
The contribution of the special all party joint committee of parliament created to examine the green paper which was issued early last year deserves particular mention. The report that committee submitted in November, 1975, after an extensive program of hearings, provided invaluable guidance in the framing of the present bill, both as regards its general philosophy and on innumerable points of detail. I would be remiss if I did not stress how much this bill owes to the tireless efforts of the members of the special joint committee in sifting the views they received from Canadians from so many walks of life and from so many organizations. The results of their work are in a very real sense manifest today, since very nearly all the recommendations in their report find themselves reflected in one way or another in the bill now before us.
There is a need for a new Immigration Act. Before discussing in any detail the major provisions of the bill, I can think of no better way of providing an overview of its basic intent than
March 10, 1977

to list some of the essential features of the bill, contrasting these with the situation existing under the present act of 1952.
The bill in clause 3 lays down in clear terms the basic objectives which the government considers should govern Canadian immigration policy now and in the future. This statement of objectives is not a pious preamble but an integral part of the proposed act. The substantive provisions of the bill flow directly from one or more of the objectives established in this clause. What the bill does here, then, is to establish a charter for the entire legislation edifice. Clause 3 is the foundation, not only for the bill itself, but for the regulations which will be made under the statute.
This, I think, is a most important innovation. The present act contains no such statement of positive purpose. It is anomalous that the law on which such an important social and economical program rests should be silent about the positive purposes immigration must promote. The current law merely tabulates methods for controlling the entry of people to this country. This bill, however, sets out the essential reasons why Canada is a country of immigration, states the underlying principles that must inspire this major program, and specifies the national goals which all our activities in the field of immigration must be designed to support.
I will have occasion to refer again to this key provision of the bill. I wish for the moment simply to draw attention to the fact that for the first time immigration law will enshrine such fundamental principles an non-discrimination, respect for the family, humanitarian concern for refugees, and the promotion of national economic, demographic, social and cultural goals.
Secondly, the bill abolishes a host of provisions which are totally archaic and unjust. Although there are many points at which the current act is outdated, this is particularly true in its approach to the prohibited classes. The present act, which has remained virtually unamended since it was passed in 1952, contains prohibitions that are universally acknowledged to be harsh and incompatible with contemporary Canadian values. The bill removes these offensive prohibitions, notably the bar against epileptics, the mentally retarded, and those who have been inmates in mental institutions. It also replaces the obsolete criterion of "moral turpitude" with objective criteria based on the provisions of Canada's Criminal Code.
Thirdly, in contrast to the present statute, which makes the crucial question of the volume of the immigration movement entirely a matter for administrative decision, the bill establishes a system under which the level of immigration to this country will become a matter for open decision making by the government in consultation with the provinces.
Fourth, the present act confers very wide regulation-making authority on the government and the minister, and is deficient in the guidance it provides for the exercise of discretion by immigration officers. The new act rectifies this unsatisfactory situation. It establishes through the statement of objectives an explicit policy framework to which everything done under the authority of the legislation must conform; and it spells out precisely and circumscribes specifically the ground to be covered by regulations.
Immigration
In the present act, the 1952 act, there is almost a basket clause which gives the minister almost unlimited authority to pass regulations to do almost anything he wishes to do so far as controlling immigration to Canada is concerned. That, I suggest, is wrong, and it is why we have changed it and been so careful in the bill to spell out the authority over the regulations which will flow from the bill.
Fifth, given the important place which refugee policy occupies in Canada's immigration practice and our outstanding record in assisting refugees, it is a curious fact that the present act makes no mention of this subject. The bill incorporates for the first time in Canadian law a regime for protecting refugees in conformity with our obligations under the United Nations convention, and establishes a refugee class.
Sixth, the bill includes measures to protect Canada against dangers, unfortunately a feature of the contemporary world, with which the provisions of the current law are inadequate to cope. In particular, it contains essential safeguards against terrorists and subversives to replace the provisions of the temporary security bill which expired at the end of this year.
Finally, the bill is sensitive to the need to safeguard the civil rights of those who are subject to immigration proceedings. Notably it introduces an important restructuring of the inquiry process as well as a more supple and humane approach to the methods for excluding or removing those persons who are found ineligible to enter or remain in this country.
Having touched on the highlights, Mr. Speaker, I should like now to discuss more fully a number of areas where the bill breaks new ground.
Dealing first with immigration levels, clause 7 requires the minister, after consultation with the provinces "and such other persons, organizations and institutions as he deems appropriate", to quote the bill, to announce annually the number of immigrants which the government considers Canada should admit over a specified time period. This important provision responds to two distinct but closely related considerations. It implements the system I mentioned earlier of open management by the government of immigration volume, which will replace the practice of essentially administrative control, which has thus far governed the total number of immigrants Canada admits. And it will permit the government to give effect to one of the important objectives stipulated in clause 3, namely, that immigration should be related to long-term planning with respect to the growth of Canada's population.
Let me deal first with the question of management. In a central recommendation, the report of the special joint committee concluded that, and I quote:
There should be a shift from the present immigration system which permits the admission of everyone meeting certain criteria without regard to total numbers, to a more managed system capable of regulating the total flow.
From the public debate the special joint committee drew the conclusion, rightly I think, that most Canadians believe that there should be a legislative means to predetermine the rate and volume of immigration to this country. The public debate revealed no clear consensus as to what that volume should be. But there is wide agreement that our immigration system

March 10, 1977
Immigration
should not be open-ended as to numbers, and that it would be desirable that, within a system which makes full provision for consultation, family reunification and the non-discriminatory application of selection procedures, the government's intentions with respect to the total volume of immigration should be the subject of an open policy determination. Within the framework of the act, clause 7 fully respects these considerations.
Over the post-war period the volume of immigration to Canada has fluctuated widely, ranging from a high of 280,000 in 1957 to a low of just over 70,000 in the early sixties. Wide year-to-year fluctuations in immigration volume are undesirable on several grounds. They complicate rational labour market planning, impose unpredictable strains on community services such as housing, schooling and the like, and render difficult sound decisions with respect to the deployment of immigrant processing resources abroad. It will be one of the government's objectives in implementing the new system of setting immigration levels in advance to avoid the high peaks and low valleys which have characterized immigration patterns in the past.
A highly significant aspect of this new arrangement will be its contribution to the creation of a new era of collaboration between the federal government and provincial governments in the immigration field. Immigration is a national program which must be responsive to the needs of all regions of Canada. Constitutionally it is a field which, while it has primacy of jurisdiction, the central government shares with the provinces. Annually announced immigration levels will be the visible end product of a regular and mandatory process of federal-provincial consultation which I am convinced will make the future administration of the program more sensitive than heretofore to the aspirations and requirements of all parts of the country.
Besides improving our capacity to manage the immigration movement in conformity with shorter-run requirements, economic and other, the advance determination of immigration levels will establish an indispensable framework for planning long-term demographic growth nationally. Whereas the minister, in accordance with clause 7, will be required each year to announce a forward figure for immigration, I envisage that the specified period covered by the announcement might well be longer than a single 12-month period. Thus, for example, in making his annual announcement the minister may find it appropriate, in the light of the consultation he has held, to announce a planning level covering a five-year period. This figure in turn would be subject to revision in the annual announcements he would be making in subsequent years.
Accordingly the arrangement will allow a very considerable measure of flexibility in determining both the actual level of immigration in any given year, as well as an opportunity to revise the longer-term level in the light of changing circumstances. It would obviously be a serious error to lock ourselves into any set figure with respect to the contribution immigration should make to Canada's population growth. Our system

must respect the fact that the factors that go to make up population policy are dynamic, variable, and unpredictable. Equally, we should be in a position to plan ahead in the light of the best data available at any given moment, and after full consultation with all those institutions of our society with a vital interest and responsibilities in the immigration process.
Since introducing the immigration bill on November 24, Mr. Speaker, I have been frequently asked what figure the government intends to set with respect to the future level of immigration to Canada. From what I have just said, I hope members appreciate that this question may betray a certain misunderstanding as to the basic purpose of this legislation. It is not its purpose to enable this or any other government to fix for all time some preconceived "ideal" number for immigration to Canada. If there is a "right" figure it will emerge only after consultation, and will be set only in the light of a judgment as to the national interest given the circumstances then prevailing.
But I acknowledge that members may properly expect me to indicate the results of the demographic studies we have pursued over the past few years, and the preliminary conclusions we have reached after discussing this subject with provincial authorities. As my predecessor in this portfolio has more than once suggested publicly, our general conclusion is that, of all the options open to Canada at the present time, the case for a moderate rate of population growth is the best. Canada's position internationally as a major food producing country, our estimate of future energy demands, the need to upgrade both the quantity and quality of housing-these are only a few of the most significant factors that have entered the government's calculation in reaching this conclusion.
It is through immigration that federal policy operates most immediately on population growth. Immigration has been an increasingly important component of annual population growth over recent years. If fertility rates remain at or close to current low levels, an annual figure for immigration from now until the census year 2001 equal to the post-war immigration average to date would mean that the Canadian population would grow from its present level of around 23 million to between 28 and 30 million by the end of the century. Expressed as an average yearly growth rate, this would represent approximately 1 per cent annually, which compares to the 1974 rate of 1.6 per cent.
This rate of population increase would, in the government's view, fairly meet the criterion of moderate growth, as contrasted to either a slow or accelerated rate. Translated into immigration figures, it would indicate an average-and I stress the word average-range of something of the order of 140,000 to
150,000	immigrants annually. Last year we received 149,429 immigrants.
Clearly I would envisage considerable year-to-year variations from such an average, either upwards or downwards, according to national requirements, including unforeseen refugee developments, and so on, although as I have said, we would aim to avoid violent fluctuations. But the main point, I hope, is evident: the government's present view of the role
March 10, 1977

immigration should play in Canada's futute population growth does not entail any departure from the position Canada has occupied since the end of the last war as a significant immigrant-receiving country.
One of the demographic characteristics which will affect the future well-being of Canadian society, the distribution of our population geographically is likely to prove just as significant as its total size, if not more so. In common with the situation in most countries, Canada is becoming increasingly a country of city-dwellers. Should present trends continue, between 80 and 90 per cent of our people will be concentrated in urban centres by the year 2000, as compared to 75 per cent at the time of the last census in 1971.
All the available evidence points to the heavy costs associated with the over-concentration of population on the one hand, and its inevitable concomitant, de-population, on the other. The achievement of more satisfactory distribution patterns for Canada's population poses formidable problems, but it is a challenge which I believe all levels of government must take up. There are very recent indications that metropolitan growth rates may be tapering off somewhat. If indeed such a trend is in the making, it must be encouraged and strengthened.
Although the federal government can provide leadership in this field, most of the levers that directly affect settlement patterns are in the hands of the provinces. For example, resource development and land use policies in general fall within provincial jurisdiction. Accordingly, to develop and implement a long-term strategy to promote the most beneficial distribution of Canada's population, active collaboration between all levels of government is imperative. Eventually, I can envisage federal-provincial agreements as providing a framework through which we could jointly work to achieve national demographic goals.
Meanwhile the government believes that immigration law should be framed in such a way that the immigration program can support whatever policies are developed in collaboration with the provinces to promote the most rational distribution of Canada's population over the years to come. I reject the notion that immigration is either the cause of population imbalances, or that immigration can be the solution. At the same time it is evident that a wider dispersal over the long term of the immigrant movement would be advantageous as we seek to restrain the forces behind metropolitan expansion, and favour the development of smaller communities.
Elere the cardinal principle to which I subscribe is that people, whether native-born Canadians or immigrants, follow opportunities. The best and most effective way to encourage immigrants to make their new homes away from the major centres is to provide incentives for them to do so-employment prospects, schools, a welcoming community. In addition, I concur with the special joint committee's conclusion that our selection standards should accord some weight in favour of those who are willing and qualified to take jobs in communities which have been designated, after federal-provincial consultation, for expansion in population. It should be self-evident that the process of designating communities for this purpose will
Immigration
require very careful study. It would be both wrong and futile to steer newcomers to Canada toward places which did not afford the prospect of a full and satisfactory life in every sense.
The new immigration legislation will do three specific things to assist a wider settlement pattern for immigrants. First, it provides for immigrants to receive their status as permanent residents-landing, as we call it-when they arrive at the destination in Canada which they chose when they were selected abroad. This would be a change from the present practice of granting landing at the port of entry, which more often than not is an airport in one of our major cities. This change may, we believe, operate as a modest factor in encouraging immigrants to stick to the destination they gave during the selection process, rather than changing plans and settling immediately elsewhere.
Secondly, it is the government's intention that the revised selection standards-the points system-which will be the subject of regulations under the new act, will include selection points which may be awarded an immigrant who is destined to a designated community. The application of the selection criteria in this respect, and the priorities which will be applied to facilitate the movement of certain categories of immigrants, are matters which I assume will be discussed in detail when the legislation is in committee.
Thirdly, clause 14 will allow an immigration officer to attach such conditions as may be prescribed in detail under the act to the grant of landing. In so far as the question of settlement is concerned, for example, this would allow a residence requirement of up to six months in the case of an immigrant who has been selected as a result of the additional points received for the designated community factor, and who benefits from priority processing as a result.
It may also be found advantageous to prescribe conditions in certain other areas. For instance, an immigrant selected because he or she agreed to take up a specific prearranged job could be granted landing on the condition that this specified employment undertaking was fulfilled. The bill provides that any such conditions in the case of immigrants would expire automatically after six months, and affords ample opportunity, if reasonable grounds exist, for the immigrant to seek relief from or changes to the conditions imposed.
Immigration law must regulate the admission, not only of the immigrant but also of the millions of people who visit Canada each year for some short-term purpose. Clause 3 of the bill acknowledges that one of the purposes of immigration policy is to facilitate the entry of visitors into Canada for the purpose of fostering trade and commerce, tourism, cultural and scientific activities, and international understanding. At the same time it is important to ensure that the welcome Canada extends visitors is not abused.
The special joint committee was impressed by the need to prevent our immigration system being circumvented by people coming to Canada as visitors with the intention of residing and working here illegally. The bill, I believe, meets the concerns

March 10, 1977
Immigration
expressed by the committee on this score. It makes it a specific offence for an employer knowingly to hire a person who is not authorized to work here. This provision ties in with the new social insurance number system, which identifies persons who are not Canadian citizens or permanent residents, and thus alerts the employer that he must verify that the person concerned is in possession of a valid employment visa.
Again following a recommendation of the special joint committee, the bill requires every visitor who wishes either to work or to study in Canada to obtain the requisite authorization from a visa officer overseas before seeking admission. With few exceptions, which will be specified in regulations, visitors already within Canada will not be eligible to apply to take temporary employment or to enrol in educational institutions. Any visitor who, without the necessary authorization, takes employment or enrols in a course of study becomes liable to deportation.
There are other provisions in the bill which complement this scheme and reinforce the basic principle that visitors enter and remain in Canada as a matter of privilege.
To balance the measures designed to combat illegal immigration, the bill introduces new bonding and security deposit provisions designed to facilitate the admission of those visitors who may find it difficult to satisfy the examining officer at the port of entry as to the purpose of their visit. Under the present law an officer is empowered to take a cash bond from the person concerned in such cases as a guarantee that he or she will leave Canada when the authorized period of the visit expires. This bill extends the type and source of security which may be deposited to cover security, other than cash, which may be deposited either by the person seeking admission or by a third party, such as a friend or relative in Canada. In brief, the bill provides for greater control over potential illegal migrants, without adding to the requirements which must be met by the genuine visitor.
As I indicated at the beginning of my remarks, the bill introduces a number of significant procedures designed to guarantee the fair treatment of those persons who may become subject to exclusion or removal from Canada. In the first place, it eliminates the present distinction between persons coming from overseas, who enjoy inquiry and have the right to counsel, and those coming from the United States or St. Pierre and Miquelon who are subject to a truncated procedure, known in the present law as a "further examination", with no right to counsel. The bill makes the full inquiry a universal procedure, regardless of the country from which the person seeks admission to Canada.
A very important change concerns the restructuring of the inquiry process itself. The special inquiry officer will be replaced by an adjudicator who will be entirely removed from the process of developing the case against an individual subject to inquiry. The adjudicator's role will be to weigh the evidence adduced by the departmental presenting officer on the one hand and the person subject to inquiry or his or her counsel on the other. The duty of the adjudicator will be to act solely as
(Mr. Cullen.)
an objective and impartial judge, to hear all the evidence, and to reach a decision according to the law.
I should also mention that the bill introduces new provisions with regard to detention which will afford individuals who are detained under the Immigration Act safeguards similar to those found in the Bail Reform Act.
Finally, I should draw attention to the alternatives to deportation which the bill provides. At a port of entry where the grounds for exclusion are relatively minor, the adjudicator will be able to issue an exclusion rather than a deportation order. The effect of the exclusion order will be to bar the return of the person to Canada for 12 months only; a deportation order, which will be used in more serious cases, will continue to constitute a permanent bar to admission unless the minister gives consent.
Similarly, if a visitor already in Canada is found at inquiry to be removable, the adjudicator may issue a departure notice rather than a deportation order when only minor infractions of the immigration law are involved. Once the person has left Canada in accordance with the terms of the departure notice, it has no further effect and the person needs no consent to apply for admission at a later date.
Included in the statement of objectives in clause 3 is the recognition that immigration policy must protect the safety of Canadian society, and should deny the use of Canadian territory to those who may engage in criminal activity. This objective is implemented in revisions to the inadmissible classes which will enable us to deal more surely with the risks presented by the contemporary phenomenon of international terrorism, highjacking, kidnapping and the like. These revisions will also enable us to deal effectively with persons seeking to enter Canada who are known to be involved with organized crime but who may have eluded conviction.
It is a characteristic of cases in the categories I have just mentioned that problems arise because evidence at the government's disposal cannot be divulged at a normal inquiry for security reasons. It will be recalled that parliament, through the passage of the Temporary Immigration Security Act, acknowledged that there were loopholes in the law in this area which needed to be closed. This bill rationalizes the manner in which these difficult cases will be handled in the future, and provides as many procedural safeguards for the individual concerned as are consistent with the overriding need to protect the safety of Canada and Canadians.
Where it is a security case involving a permanent resident, the bill establishes very special procedures. The current law provides for the deportation of a landed immigrant through the inquiry process, but does not adequately cover those very serious security cases which preclude resort to that procedure. Accordingly, the bill makes provisions for a special advisory board which will consider evidence submitted by the Minister of Manpower and Immigation and the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox). The individual concerned will be given an opportunity to be heard in accordance with regulations which will resemble those set out in the Public Service Security Inquiry Regulations. If the board is satisfied that grounds for removal exist, it
March 10, 1977

will report to the governor in council which may make the necessary deportation order.
There are several important aspects of this legislation which deserve more attention but which it is impossible for me to cover adequately at this time. Because of the complexity of some of these issues, I believe that their detailed examination had best be reserved for the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, to which I hope it will be possible to refer the bill after appropriate debate, and where it would be my intention to discuss the substance of the more important regulations. One complicated area which I know the committee will wish to discuss in detail is the regime the bill provides to protect refugees.
Another less complex area, but about which some concern and misunderstanding have become evident, is the provision in the bill which can require persons other than Canadian citizens to be fingerprinted under certain circumstances. Many immigrant-receiving countries routinely require applicants for visas to be fingerprinted. We certainly do not intend to go that far. Fingerprinting will be the exception rather than the rule, used only where there is doubt about a person's identity or his possible involvement in criminal activity. For persons in Canada we will fingerprint as a matter of routine only those who have been ordered removed from Canada. The two other situations in which we will require fingerprints are when a person is arrested under the Immigration Act, or when a visitor requests a change in or extension to his status, and, in either case, the person is unable to satisfy the immigration officer of his identity. It will therefore be a rarity for a permanent resident to be fingerprinted. In all cases, when the fingerprints have served their immigration purpose, they will be disposed of under the normal file retirement program.
Another complicated area which the committee will wish to study in detail is the revision of the selection standards which, of course, will be a matter for regulations. On this subject I will only say now that the recommendations of the special joint committee appear to provide a very solid basis for a new points system.
I cannot neglect to mention at this time the strident criticism of the bill put about by a few small groups in Toronto and Montreal, claiming that the bill is racist, discriminatory, repressive, and reduces the civil rights of visitors, immigrants and citizens alike. I have examined those accusations in some detail, being alarmed by their shrillness. I am satisfied that the groups concerned have not only misinterpreted the bill's provisions, but I have also been forced to the sad conclusion that their reports constitute a deliberate and shocking attempt to discredit the bill. I propose, if the committee has any interest in pursuing the matter, to demonstrate to the members the exaggerated and frequently completely invalid nature of those criticisms.
In these remarks I have not addressed the question of family immigration, since the government's present intentions with respect to the expansion of the family class and the admission
Immigration
of more distant relatives were the subject of a communication addressed to all members at the time I introduced the bill. In brief, the new family class will include those relatives who are now sponsorable, plus parents of any age when sponsored by Canadian citizens. Additionally, the government proposes that those relatives eligible for nomination will continue to receive under the new regulations the same level of preference they now enjoy.
It only remains for me to say that I am convinced that this legislation will provide a strong and imaginative foundation on which to conduct Canada's immigration program in the future.
I wish again to express my appreciation to those members on both sides of the House who have already made a significant contribution to this bill through their participation in the special joint committee. I trust that the standing committee can complete its examination of the bill during the first months of the new year to enable the House and the Senate to pass the legislation by the middle of 1977.
I would also be remiss if I did not comment on the splendid work and service performed on behalf of that committee by one of its co-chairman, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. O'Connell).

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to represent my party today in opening debate on Bill C-24. I intend to direct some of my remarks to the speech of the minister, but primarily I will leave some of the areas he touched for debate at committee stage.
Public affairs tend to concentrate on immediate problems and very often address themselves only to short-term solutions. The attention of the public and the attention of the public media generally focus on the immediate. As a result governments and public officials frequently are seen to lurch from crisis to crisis. The accusation that we do not spend sufficient time and thought on issues which require long-term solutions is frequently made. The issue before us today addresses itself to Canada's future, and I believe the minister was correct in stating that it will have long-term implications for many generations to come.
As the official representative of my party I intend to outline our position on Canada's demographic policy. In order to do that I believe it is essential that we review the process by which we have arrived at this point. It is only in the historical context that we are able to evaluate Canada's development. It is the lessons of history which enable us to project possible future developments.
Canada is a land of immigrants. This phenomenon dates back to our colonial history. Not only were France and England concerned about development of Canada's economic resources and population base, but even more so in more modern times administrations of both Conservative and Liberal political affiliation saw the need for the development of Canada's population. They were also concerned about the enrichment of that population. As we make plans for Canada's future and established population goals, we as Canadians

March 10, 1977
Immigration
should view this task with enthusiasm rather than fear. It is a task filled with great potential. It is a task which will affect the lives of our children and grandchildren. To put it in simple terms, the policies we establish today will affect the future of our children.
What kind of Canada do we want to see developed? Before one can answer that question, Canadians and the government must have a clear sense of national priority. Just as Canada's history is marked by periods when national priorities gripped the attention and captured the enthusiasms of Canadians, so the time has come for us once again to establish a national goal. This national goal must be to develop a demographic policy which will ensure a future for all Canadians in which not only economic opportunities will exist but, more important, where principles of freedom, racial equality, and justice will prevail for everyone.
While these goals are high sounding and by their very nature nebulous, this is a task to which we must address ourselves. It is of utmost importance that the process of consultation between the federal government, the provincial governments, and Canadians generally takes place. Not only must this consultative process be on a regular and ongoing basis, but it must be meaningful, and the consultation must take place in the open. If we fail in this task, we fail in the greatest challenge facing us today.
At the time the green paper on immigration was tabled in the House indications were given by the government that Canada's immigration policy would be examined as an integral part of the larger demographic policy. At that time our party called for a select committee to be established, the responsibility of which would be to do the following: first, to examine immigration policy up to the present time; second, to examine the main principles of Canadian demographic policy of the future; and third, to conduct hearings across Canada, thus ensuring the input of Canadians in this all-important question. As I look around the House tonight it is with interest that I see many members of parliament who sat on that committee as it travelled across Canada.
I believe all of us admired people who had come to this country, and we were filled with admiration when we saw the loyalty and the love they held for this country. We were particularly impressed with their determination to make Canada a better place in which to live.
At the time the green paper was tabled our party criticized the government because we felt that insufficient attention had been paid to Canada's demographic policy. Further, we stressed that Canada's immigration policy could not be examined without first establishing our demographic goals. That accusation was valid in 1973, and I suggest that it is still valid today in 1977. Again the government has failed to follow that advice. Instead, we are faced with an immigration bill, and while reference is made to demographic policy, and while the minister addressed himself to that question superficially tonight, it is our view that demographic principles are again taking secondary importance to that of amending present immigration legislation.
I Mr. Epp.]
The government has attempted to create the impression that it is dedicated to a demographic policy. It has taken great pains to stress that demographic considerations are extremely important. The bill states demographic studies as one of its objects in clause 3, and stresses provincial consultation regarding demographics in clause 7. Yet when the minister is asked to table the report on demographic studies so that members of parliament can make an educated assessment of the bill, the minister's response is that he will consider it. I was under the impression that at second reading the minister would table demographic projections. He had an opportunity to do that today, but he failed to do so.
I suggest to the minister, as forcefully as I can, that we want the regulations before us during second reading debate, and also the principles upon which his demographic projections were based. If in fact demographic and population policy is to be one of the major factors affecting the determination of immigration levels, and perhaps even the points system, then all these factors must be evaluated as an integral part of the new immigration legislation. I must reiterate that the entire selection system by which immigrants will come to Canada is not part of the bill. This means that it is not open for debate. It is our intention to place the selection system, the points system, in the bill through an amendment in order that all future Canadians may clearly understand the manner in which they would have to qualify to come to Canada.
At the present time world population stands at approximately four billion, with an annual growth rate of approximately 2 per cent. World population, if this trend continues, will be doubled in approximately 35 years. Even if the fertility rate were to decrease to replacement levels by as early as 1980, the world would still have an increase in population to 6.3 billion in 75 years time. In order to appreciate the enormity of the problem, if the replacement level were reached by the turn of the century, a goal which is more possible than the 1980 supposition, the world's population would number approximately eight billion by the year 2050.
The average net increase on a world basis today is 200,000 people per day. Further, adding to the world pressure is the fact that over 90 per cent of any future growth will take place in the underdeveloped countries. This increased pressure on the world population adds to the task of finding sufficient resources. Despite the tremendous increase in world population, world energy conversion is increasing three times faster than the world's population. We all speak of energy conservation, but still the fact remains that in spite of rapidly developing world population, the conversion of world energy supplies is increasing three times more rapidly than the world's population.

speechtext: What would you do?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
Again I am asked what we would do. I can tell the hon. member that what we would do would be a sight better than they have ever done.
The 1960's saw marked increases in the development of the world's food supply. The so-called green revolution spelled hope for millions of persons in underdeveloped countries that they might at least look forward to the day where they would receive daily nourishment. Unfortunately the race to increase food production more rapidly than the world's population increase is now also being lost. Today we are faced with the fact that despite tremendous gains in agricultural production, the world's population is again growing faster than the increase in food production.
As a partial response to an ever-increasing world population and the need to provide basic food and shelter, the world plan of action which was adopted at the Bucharest conference urged national governments to develop population policies, keeping in mind the need to develop policies which would result in some hope for the world's teaming millions. In the developed countries, opposite trends have been taking place.
Hon. members opposite ask what we would do. This is another case where they have not looked at the facts but rather rushed in with the hope that the public would buy arguments not based on present trends. Assuming that Canada's fertility rate will remain at 1.8 as is presently the case, we already are below our replacement level which is placed at 2.3, which is the average number of children a woman will bear during her child-bearing lifetime. While fertility rates are presently below replacement levels, the birth rate of 15 per 1,000 population is still double our mortality rate. With this rate plus the fact that an imbalance exists in our age structure, namely, that the postwar baby boom has resulted in a higher percentage of women of child-bearing age, it is projected that even without any immigration at all Canada's population by the year 2000 will rise to some 26 million. Having said that, one fact becomes startlingly evident, namely, that immigration will become an ever-increasingly important component in any future demographic policy.
At the present time immigration accounts for roughly half our population increase. We have to go back to the 1920's to find another trend in which immigration resulted in 50 per cent of Canada's population increase.
The joint committee travelled throughout Canada, and representations varied all the way from a closed-door policy to
Immigration
one which would allow large numbers of immigrants to enter Canada yearly. Our party has opted for neither extreme. Rather, based on the principle that immigration is a privilege, we opted for moderate growth. The joint committee on immigration put that figure at approximately 125,000; tonight the minister put it at from 140,000 to 150,000. What are the results if we look at these figures, Mr. Speaker?
If the figure of 100,000 immigrants per year was to be used in the next five years, and assuming that the fertility rate remains at 1.8, we have already indicated that our population would rise to 26 million without any immigration by the year 2000. With immigration in the area of 100,000 per year, combined with net emigration of some 50,000 per year-and I want to say to the minister that we have no adequate emigration figures in Canada at the present time-the result would be that by the year 2001 our population would be 29 million or 30 million.
Demographers project that if these trends were to continue, in the first half of the twenty-first century our population will rise to approximately 33 million before stabilizing around that figure. If one were to accept immigration figures of 200,000 per year, as is generally done by those who argue for a more open immigration policy, the higher immigration flow would result in Canada's population rising to approximately 33 million by the year 2001. The rationale for adopting a figure such as I have indicated is based on the observations I gave earlier.
A number of Canadians have also expressed the view that Canada should virtually stop all immigration. Let me point out at this time that our party applauds the contribution immigrants have made to the development of Canada. As Canadians we have prided ourselves that we have created a pluralistic society. While we favour the belief that all immigrants should have the opportunity to enter the main stream of Canadian life we have been the beneficiaries of their enthusiams, their vision, their culture, and possibly most important, Mr. Speaker, their love for their adopted country.
Those of us born in Canada often take the freedoms we enjoy in this country for granted. Those who count themselves among the members of Canada's ethnic communities cherish their Canadian home, cherish it in a way which is a lesson to all of us. Therefore we say Canada is the better for the immigrants we welcomed to our shores. We say that we need a continued flow of immigrants. Our country is going through a period of economic difficulty, going through a period of inflation and unemployment. We say that these conditions always make it more difficult for immigrants to integrate into Canadian society, but it is important that Canada should retain an immigration flow. Demographic projections indicate that if Canada's fertility rate remains low, below replacement levels, Canada will need additional people to enter the labour market by the early 1980's. By the 1980's we shall experience a sharp decline in the annual growth of the labour force, a decline between 2 per cent and 3 per cent.

March 10, 1977
Immigration
The former chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, appearing before the joint committee on immigration, said this:
This decline to a lower and more normal rate of entrance into the labour force could mean that, without immigration, future economic development might actually be held back by labour shortages.
In its 1975 study entitled "Looking Outward" the Economic Council of Canada said:
Council projections suggest therefore that the labour force including net immigration will grow by about 2.7 per cent per annum between 1975 and 1980 compared with about 3.4 per cent from 1969 to 1974, and barely 2 per cent per annum from 1980 to 1985. This slowdown is likely to continue into the 1990's. The priorities of Canadian economic policy are in consequence also likely to shift steadily to emphasize less the number of jobs available in the economy than the quality of employment provided.
As we look ahead to the 1980's and 1990's, it becomes evident that we are justified in opposing a closed door policy. Rather, we ought to encourage immigration in moderate quantities.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
The second factor which emphasizes this relates to Canada's welfare system. Since World War II, Canada has developed a comprehensive program of social welfare benefits. These benefits have long-term implications for Canada's economic growth. They are based on the assumption that not only will economic activity be able to maintain the increased costs of social welfare benefits in place, but that the growth in the labour force will be large enough to support those receiving social benefits. Consideration of this factor, more than any other, has led us to the conclusion that moderate growth is necessary. If we were not growing, or if our population growth were approaching zero, future generations in Canada would be hard-pressed to pay the cost of continuing social benefits.
Owing to the post-war baby boom, a large percentage of women now living in Canada are of child-bearing age. If the population does not increase, as the dependency factor on the population grows, that is to say, as the population grows older, a smaller percentage of people working will be asked to pay for social benefits. Surely it becomes self-evident that one of two options remains: either social benefit programs must be reduced, or continued growth of the population must take place.
Having said that, I make this point: demographers generally agree that even though additional points are provided for immigrants entering the labour force, only a natural increase will make a significant difference to Canada's age structure. One might ask why does Canada not opt for more immigrants, possibly in excess of 200,000 or 250,000 per year? The first reason relates back to a matter to which I have already addressed myself, namely, the increase in world population.
At present world population is increasing by 200,000 per day. It is evident that at no time can Canada develop an immigration policy which could significantly reduce the world's over-population problem. Rather, it is incumbent on us, as Canadians, to help in the development of agricultural techniques and resources in the developing world, in order that

those countries may develop the capacity to increase their own food production.
Further, an ever-decreasing number of countries are willing to take in significant numbers of immigrants. In the past Europe, Australia, New Zealand and North and South America were designated as receiving areas. In the latter part of the 1970's not only has the number of receiving areas been reduced, but those countries willing to receive immigrants are reducing the numbers they will allow to enter. This fact, along with the desire of much of the world's population to emigrate to countries such as Canada in the hope of economic betterment, will put additional pressure on Canada in the last quarter of the century to accept more immigrants. This trend is already evident in that Canada is receiving over 750,000 immigrant applications per year from persons expressing a desire to emigrate to Canada. It remains unclear how many more would be received if potential immigrants were not told that their chance of emigrating to Canada is virtually non-existent.
An additional argument militating against larger population increase is the question of economies of scale. Generally, it has been argued that large populations result in a larger domestic market and it therefore follows that increased economic growth is the result. The joint committee on immigration studied at length the question of economies of scale. Recent studies indicate that if significant shifts in economies of scale are to be achieved, Canada's population growth must be significant, since in developing societies every individual places additional pressures on non-renewable resources, transportation, housing, education, etc.
Traditional arguments concerning economies of scale have become less valid in today's society. One could say that Canada is the beneficiary of economies of scale-economies of scale not relating to our domestic population. I say this simply because we are a major exporting nation. Unfortunately an examination of 1976 figures reveals our trade deficit, reveals part of the reason for our economic slump. That slump has led to a loss of jobs and economic hardship in Canada. And there is hardship when a trading nation is in a deficit position.
A Canadian ecomonist, Spencer Star, wrote one of the most significant papers I have seen on this subject. After studying economies of scale he concluded that population growth is an insignificant factor in the annual growth of income per person. He also wrote that it is safe to say that population and immigration policy discussions may proceed without being concerned that a policy directed toward a relatively low population growth rate will have any measurable net loss to Canada in terms of foregone economies of scale. Similarly, there is no reason to expect a relatively high population growth rate to confer any measurable net benefits through realized economies of scale.
A further reason which militates against excessive population growth is the trend toward urbanization. Our pattern of distribution in this country can best be described as a failure. We have increased the size of our three major urban areas, Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver. Historically, immigrants
March 10, 1977

have tended to settle in large metropolitan areas. For example, Ontario receives in the neighbourhood of 55 per cent of all new immigrants to Canada, but this is only half the story. The other side of that coin is internal migration.
Internal migration has also resulted in rapid increases in the growth of Canada's urban areas. This trend again shows that the government's policies, such as those of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, have had little or no effect on significantly changing the rural to urban movement.
It is incumbent upon the government to establish policies whereby Canada's rural areas are able to attract secondary industry in order to develop a more mature economy. This would not only reduce pressure on Canada's urban areas, but would allow Canadian citizens in rural areas to develop the potential that is now only available in Canada's urban areas.
It is essential if our regions of Canada are to remain in Confederation that a more equitable distribution on a regional basis be undertaken immediately. It is self-evident why persons are attracted to Canada's urban areas. Surely it goes without saying that the main reason is employment and with it the opportunity to advance one's economic well-being. The Progressive Conservative party would develop a consultative process with the provinces and municipalities to develop policies which would allow for the same economic opportunities to be existent in Canada's less urbanized areas that presently exist in our larger urban areas.

For some time today in my speech I have dwelt on our general projections on population growth. I believe that this really is the central question that should be discussed by members on both sides of the House, but as 1 stated before, it is a question that many members shy away from because of the obvious pitfalls one can get into as one discusses demographic policy.
As one reads Bill C-24, one must agree with the general objectives as stated in clause 3. Let me draw specific attention to some with which we completely agree. We are pleased that they are incorporated into a bill and will now have the power of law rather than be simply good intentions.
This is a day of which we should all be proud, a day in which we are getting a bill which clearly states that Canada's immigration goal is, and I quote:
(c)	to facilitate the reunion in Canada of Canadian citizens and permanent residents with their close relatives from abroad;
(d)	to encourage and facilitate the adaptation of persons who have been granted admission as permanent residents to Canadian society-
Also, we finally have a refugee policy that is included in the legislation. The joint committee clearly stated that these objectives should be in legislation. I commend the minister, and possibly even more so his predecessor, on those objectives being included in the bill.
Immigration
It is our view that much more openness must exist between the federal and provincial governments in discussion of immigration policies. This is possibly where we have our greatest objection to the minister and Bill C-24. While the minister gives lip service to openness, there is not much more openness in Bill C-24 than in the 1952 act. Why do I say this?
The minister says there will be a consultative process with the provinces. The minister has indicated that immigration is a shared responsibility with the provinces but the prime responsibility rests with the federal government. The minister has not placed before us any projections, or agreements that have been made between the federal government and the provinces. The minister might say that that is impossible at this time. While that might be the case and we can possibly accept that, the mechanisms and the consultative process are not before us once again. It goes without saying that if the provinces have to bear the cost of additional housing, transportation and education, it is incumbent that the provinces have input in this consultative process. We are not interested in balkanizing the various regions of Canada, but we are interested in recognizing the special needs that immigrants have and the special problems immigration resettlement programs bring to the provinces.
Further, Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate that as a party we do not feel it is sufficient that the minister should simply announce the annual level. Rather, we are proposing an amendment whereby the minister not only will have to announce the annual level, but will table a report in the House of Commons, and further that this report will be referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration for debate and review, thus enabling the committee not only to question the appropriate minister as to the reasons the level was established in quantitative terms, but also on the projections the minister has for the future of the demographic policy.
When my colleague from Hamilton' West (Mr. Alexander) spoke of immigration, he had a favourite phrase to describe Canada's immigration policy. He called it legislation by regulation. Bill C-24 follows in that tradition. To a great extent it is legislation by regulation. Having said that, there is not much disagreement with what the bill says in its philosophy. But Bill C-24 is even more important in what it does not say. For one, the regulations are not written into the bill. While I recognize that all regulations cannot be written into the bill, I believe that selection criteria, annual targets, demographic targets, mechanisms and how they are to be modified, should be included in the bill. This is of particular significance in terms of the points system.
In other words the minister has structured the bill in such a way that there will be no opportunity for meaningful debate on the mechanics of immigration. Therefore it is the view of my party that the government has been dishonest in its public portrayal that the bill is open. The bill is grossly lacking in that it gives no indication as to the selection system. In fact if any meaningful debate is to take place, I want to stress again

March 10, 1977
Immigration
that the regulations must be made available during second reading debate and in committee.
The very nature of the immigration department indicates that it is regulatory in nature. It is essential that those regulations be placed before us. As one reads the act, one can only conclude that in some ways it is more arbitrary than the previous one in that it places even more power in the hands of the minister and the bureaucrats.
If one wants to look at the bureaucratic jungle created by Bill C-24, one comes to the conclusion that immigration policies will become more confusing and therefore more discriminatory and more unfair. I simply cannot accept that persons in the department who are generally manpower oriented have the same perception for immigration needs as persons who would be responsible to a department of immigration and citizenship, as opposed to the monstrosity the minister is now proposing.
I base that on the white paper on immigration which the government tabled in 1966. That report was tabled after two years of study to review all aspects of immigration. As one reads that paper of some years ago, one notices that the government's observation of Canada's economic future was expansionary in nature. The philosophy was one of a great future. It stressed the traditional reasons to encourage immigration. While it concerned itself with a selection system as it pertains to immigration, its message was clear: Canada's economic future was bright, and immigrants not only would contribute to that economic future but would share in it.
That was in 1966, and 10 years later, with the same government, what has happened? The government's economic policies are in a shambles and the government has to retreat. I say to the bureaucrats in the manpower area that again their projections in 1966 have not been found to be factual in 1977.
Now, Mr. Speaker, what about the selection criteria? This is one of the objections that we have to Bill C-24. At the present time three categories exist for immigrant classification, namely, the sponsored, nominated, and family class. Clause 115, while designating the classes, indicates the manner in which persons will now be selected based on future regulation. Therefore one has to look at the minister's press release that accompanied the tabling of Bill C-24 in order to discover the new selection system. The special joint committee, after reviewing the selection system at length-and I repeat, Mr. Speaker-at length-generally agreed that the sponsored class should remain, or rather that it now be called the family class.
In fact the committee said, to quote from the committee report:
To ensure this all committee members except one recommend that the present class of the nominated immigrant be dropped and that the ties between members of a non-dependent extended family be recognized a different way.
After lengthy debate in the committee, the committee recommended, based on the principle of family reunification, that the family class should remain and that parents of any age could be placed in the sponsored class, as presently they

must be at least 60 years of age before they can be sponsored. It was on that basis that the committee recommended expansion of the sponsored class and also recommended the removal of the nominated class.
It is our recommendation that the present sponsored class be expanded to include parents at any age; but when one reads the press release of the minister, not only is it parents of any age but grandparents as well. I do not know if the minister or his officials have in fact studied the ripple effect of that change, but I suggest to him that if he sets annual targets at between 100,000 and 140,000 per year, the ripple effect could be such that hardly any independent immigrants, or what he prefers to term "others", will have an opportunity to come to Canada.

speechtext: You are referring to nominated?

subtopic: IMMIGRATION ACT, 1976 AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT CHANGES IN IMMIGRATION POLICY
speechtext:
The minister asks if I am referring to nominated. The present bill has a family class which has now been expanded, or which the minister says, if we are to take his word, will be expanded to include parents of any age and grandparents. The committee also recommended that the nominated class be removed. Now, Mr. Speaker, the minister has done that, but he has not. He has retained the points for the nominated class. The committee, after lengthy discussion of this question, indicated that new seed immigration would be severely hampered if annual targets were established, and that most immigrants who came to Canada would qualify to come to Canada through prior family connection.
It is new seed immigration, Mr. Speaker, which longitudinal studies indicate will more readily move to areas outside our metropolitan cities. While the minister has reduced the nominated class or eliminated it, he has retained the points which are presently in the nominated class, and I believe that that is something that must seriously be looked at by the committee.
As to the second class, Mr. Speaker, we favour the inclusion of a refugee class. It is the first time, I believe, in Canada's immigration policy that, by legislation, Canada confirms its obligations which we have undertaken as a signatory of the United Nations Convention and Protocol on Refugees. As a party we favour this inclusion in the bill. As refugee situations frequently demand immediate and direct attention, one has to ask whether Canada should establish a policy whereby we are a country of first asylum. A number of representations were made that Canada accept the principle of being a country of first asylum. This would mean that persons who claim refugee status could enter Canada and remain here on a minister's permit until such time as we could determine whether in fact they were refugees under the terms of the UN charter.
Proponents of this concept generally refer to the Swedish experience, but the point must be made that Sweden only accepts 1,000 refugees per year, and Canada's record is much more exemplary than that of Sweden. Therefore, we see no reason why Canada should accept the proposal that it be designated as a country of first asylum. It is our view that in a world where increased tensions will take place, especially
March 10, 1977

within countries, pressures to accept increased refugee flows will remain with us for some time.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, regarding selection, the category of other immigrants, as the minister's press release describes them, would be comprised of all applicants who do not qualify under the family class or as refugees. Again, Mr. Speaker, these people ought to be judged on the points system, which again is not included in the bill. Therefore it becomes difficult to assess the manner in which the so-called independent immigrant will be selected. It would be my view-and I hope the minister will see the wisdom of this suggestion-that these persons should not be designated as other applicants but rather as independent applicants.
I have therefore served notice on the minister and the government that we intend to move a significant number of amendments to improve Bill C-24. It is our thinking that it is the only way that changes to the points system, and therefore to the selection criteria for immigrants, can in future be debated in parliament. We have seen in the last two or three years that significant changes to regulations have taken place without any debate in the Elouse of Commons, and therefore without any input by Canadians or their representatives.
Regarding the so-called inadmissible classes, I am pleased to note that exclusion of potential immigrants will be based solely on danger to public health or safety, or excessive demands on health or social services, to quote the bill. In the past, as the House knows, the 1952 act barred epileptics and those suffering from mental disease. Many of the provisions in section 5 of the 1952 act were, as the minister has already said, archaic. There is agreement that members of families should not be separated because one member of a family suffers from mental retardation. Therefore the special joint committee recommended that sponsored dependents who are mentally retarded should be admissible. Further, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to note that those suffering from epilepsy will not be placed in the prohibited class any longer.
A matter a deep concern to our party, though, is the question of illegal aliens. I have already stated that additional pressures will be placed on Canada in that persons view Canada as a land of opportunity. Generally, there are two types of illegal aliens seeking to enter Canada. The first category we have seen, for example, arrive at our major airports having left their home under the impression that they can enter Canada as visitors and also find work, in many cases. Having arrived in Canada many of them find themselves bitterly disappointed. When these persons arrive at Canada's international airports, frequently they have little or no financial resources with which to maintain themselves for the period of time they intend to stay in this country. The result is that they are detained and placed in detention centres until a special inquiry takes place the next day or so, and they are then sent back to their country of origin. Many of these people are unfortunate victims of misinformation or, even worse, of travel agencies who indicate to them that if they have a return ticket in their pocket they will automatically be allowed to remain in Canada.
Immigration
Those of us who have seen these detention centres know that a better method must be developed in order to reduce the heartbreak of these persons and their relatives and friends in Canada. The excessive amounts of money that are needed for them to travel to Canada add additional hardships on these persons. Therefore a visitor visa system must be developed whereby a person must attain an entry visa before being allowed into Canada. These visas would be made available at Canadian embassies abroad. As a starting point, 1 suggest this be done on a reciprocal basis with countries which themselves presently require an entry or exit card system. The same system might be adopted with respect to visitors from those countries to Canada.
The second group of illegal entrants are those who have been able to escape the secondary line of inspection and enter the mainstream of Canadian life. Estimates as to their number vary, but range as high as half a million. I do not know how many there are, and the minister keeps saying there are no projections. If a visa system were devised we would at least have some idea as to the number of visitors present in Canada at any time.
It is the view of my party that the government has lost control of the illegal alien question. Examining the situation, especially in Canada's urban areas, immigration officers indicate they do not possess the resources to enable them to cope with the illegal alien who is able to escape immigration controls. Studies in Toronto indicate that many illegal aliens who are eventually detained have already worked in Canada for an average of one year. Officials indicate that they lack the proper training or equipment to do the job they are required to do. Also, a number of these illegal immigrants are engaged in criminal activity.
It goes without saying that the illegal immigrant has often been a victim of extortion. I was pleased to hear the minister state that Canadians who knowingly employ illegal immigrants will also be subject to prosecution. There is a feeling abroad in Canada that another amnesty program will be undertaken, possibly at the time the new bill is proclaimed. In 1972 when the amnesty program was announced, that program received support from my party. I want to say very clearly this evening that an amnesty program to make legal that which is illegal will not receive support at this time from the Official Opposition. I also wish to stress that additional steps must be taken to screen out persons engaged in organized crime. Immigration officials have expressed fears to me that this is an ever-increasing problem.
I do not have time to go into the substance of the bill at this point. Other members of this party will do so, but in conclusion, let me say this: as Canadians we have always prided ourselves on the development of a pluralistic society. The Immigration Act clearly states that our immigration policy is not to be discriminatory. The Bill of Rights confirms it as well. These are the principles upon which this party wants to see any future immigration policy based.
