I do not think the spokesman for the Conservative party did, but we do. We think that the right to bring in one's parents is a reasonable provision in a bill which says that one of its principles is to reunite families, but the minister is asking us to discuss this legislation without seeing the regulations.
I have mentioned only a few of the subjects which are to be dealt with by the regulations. The whole points system, setting out the qualifications and attributes for independent or nominated applicants, appears nowhere in the act. I do not know whether there will be nominated applicants. I thought I heard the minister say at an earlier date that there would be, but if so, we do not know. We do not know whether or not that will be true. We have had, and I presume we will continue to have, a points system without qualifications and attributes, but we do not know what changes have been made in that.
The joint committee, as I remember, included amongst its recommendations the suggestion that more points be given for working experience and fewer points for academic successes. I perceive these to be good provisions, but we do not know whether they will be in the regulations or not, and yet we are asked to give approval to the bill.
The minister has pointed out-and I want to say something about it later in approval-that clause 3 of the bill in fact sets out immigration objectives, but these are put in a general way. They would not take effect over the specific rules contained in the regulations. They are useful, perhaps good for assisting in the interpretation of the act and of the regulations, but in no way enforceable by law. They are just a series of well sounding and very justifiable objectives, and I am glad to see them
Immigration
there, but let us not fool ourselves that they take the place of actual, concrete legislation dealing with these matters.
The regulations may exempt any groups from the requirements of the regulations. Persons to be admitted on compassionate grounds are to be designated by regulations, not by parliament, and when we come down to the question of refugees we find that there again the standards that they are required to achieve are to be spelled out in the regulations and are not clearly enunciated in the bill. I want to say something about the refugee system later.
We provide for students coming here, but the regulations decide what educational institutions can receive students. Parliament is not asked to deal with this and to say what students from abroad should come and what type of education we think we can afford and should afford to give to people coming from outside this country.
All questions related to required documentation in respect of any visitor can be dealt with by regulations. The regulations prescribe the factors to be considered as to whether any person is likely to be a danger to public safety or whether he would be expected to cause excessive demand on health and social services. As I read clause 19(1) of the bill, a medical officer is given the ultimate right to determine whether an excessive demand on the health and social service exists.
In clause 115( 1 )(n) I find entirely different meaning in the words and the language. 1 do not know how some people manage to read into perfectly clear words limitations that are in no way stated. Clause 115(1 )(n) requires any person or class of persons to report to an immigration officer before leaving Canada and the appropriate regulations will prescribe the information to be provided and the manner in which such reports shall be made to the immigration officer by any such person. It is true that there is a note in the yellow document at the side which says that this will only be done when it is necessary for proper identification and control of the illegal immigrant. I think the minister has something to say on this. I want to impress upon him and upon members of the House that it is the act and the regulations that will count, not side notes and observations by the minister, and we should not be fobbed off with these vague, general statements.
This is a radical, new proposal-I use the word "radical" in an uncomplimentary sense-which somehow or other will require what might well be Canadians of long standing to go to an immigration officer to provide information. It is not made clear in the legislation whether the immigration officer is bound to or can refuse to give a person leave to depart from Canada. In any event, this may well be a restriction on the rights of Canadian citizens to freedom to travel, and runs counter to the declarations signed by Canada as to the right to such freedom of travel. It is a backward step, moving in the direction of a police state, to have to report to immigration officers whenever people want to leave the country, and if parliament passes this bill in this form it is not parliament which will control this matter but the regulation-making authority.

March 10, 1977
Immigration
Clause 115(1 )(o) is equally, if not more, objectionable. It enables the regulations to set out the circumstances under which a person other than a Canadian citizen seeking admission to Canada may be required to be fingerprinted and photographed. For myself, I would not feel it necessarily a serious invasion of rights if all Canadians were required to be fingerprinted for the purpose of keeping records, but I think it is wrong to select a particular group.
Hitherto we have gone on the assumption that once a person is admitted to Canada for permanent residence, he has the same basic rights as other Canadians. This clause will cause extremely hard feelings amongst ethnic groups affected and will alarm all those who believe in civil liberties.
Clause 14 provides that if an immigration officer is satisfied that it would not be contrary to the legislation or the regulations to grant admission, he may grant admission and impose terms and conditions. What kinds of terms and conditions? Are they spelled out in the legislation? No, they are not. They are terms and conditions of a prescribed nature, which is another way of saying prescribed by regulations and not by parliament. Once again the government has the power to impose these terms and conditions through an order in council and without interference by parliament.
It might be said that to object to provisions because the bill contains regulations rather than incorporating the law in the main legislation is a question of formality and without substance, but the truth is different. The effect of transferring powers of legislation to the governor in council means that the basic rules as to immigrants can be dealt with through the normal bureacratic process in an almost secretive way, and very often without adequate public notice.
On a matter as sensitive and as important as immigration, the basic rules should be made and set out by parliament itself.
I want to illustrate the sweeping nature of these regulations. There has been a very substantial decline in the number of people admitted to Canada as immigrants. That is not due to any will of parliament, and it was not discussed in parliament. It is due to a regulation passed on October 22, 1974, which said that independent applicants, in some cases nominated applicants, must not only arrange definitive employment, which is defined, but what was even more important, they must arrange to obtain from the national employment service-in other words, the manpower branch-a certificate saying that no Canadian citizen is willing, able or qualified for the employment in which the applicant is willing to engage in Canada.
The Standing Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments, of which I happen to be a member, in its recently filed report referred to the secretive nature of many immigration directives. I am not making this up out of my head because of some degree of hostility toward the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Far from it; I am quoting what a committee of this House representing all parties says is the fact.

When we do these things in this way the directives to which I referred are not available to the public or to the would-be immigrant. The picutre is one of great secrecy. In many cases neither the applicant nor his advisers can discover what the rules are by which their admission is being considered, and if refused, why they were refused. Under the old act and under the decisions given by the courts, an applicant was entitled to a hearing, and at the hearing the reasons for refusal of admission had to be stated. The trend has now fully developed toward the department answering all such questions with generalities such as "you do not meet the requirements" or "you are not able to establish yourself successfully in Canada." This tells the applicant absolutely nothing of the basic reasons why his application is refused.
I suggest that the whole bill be withdrawn and that there be inserted in the bill all the minor basic provisions which are necessary. As it stands, there is an ample indication by parliament that it will accept its legislative responsibilities. True, many detailed procedures can indeed be left to regulations.

HEALTH-ALLEGED REFUSAL OF CONNAUGHT LABORATORIES TO SUPPLY GAMMA GLOBULIN TO MALTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the question period on Friday, March 4, of this year I appealed to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to use his office to make available 60 vials of human gamma globulin on an emergency basis to our fellow Commonwealth country, Malta. On Wednesday, March 2, at 6 p.m. I received from the office of the Malta Trade Commission in Toronto an urgent request to help find some gamma globulin which was urgently needed in Malta. This followed a negative response from the Connaught Laboratories in Toronto.
Immediately following this urgent call I telephoned the office of the Minister of National Health and Welfare conveying this request. Forty-two hours later, after no positive response, I was compelled to raise this matter in the House by way of a question to the minister. With great disappointment I have to state this evening that my telegram of March 4 to Mr. March 10, 1977

Hampson, Chairman of the Canadian Development Corporation, which acquired the Connaught Laboratories, has not yet been answered as of this moment.
However, I am grateful that the blood transfusion service of the Canadian Red Cross answered my telegram within a few hours informing me that a gift of human gamma globulin was in the hands of the representative of the Malta Trade Commission in Toronto by 3 p.m. on Friday, March 4. On this occasion I want to thank the Canadian Red Cross for responding so quickly and so generously to this request.
However, I want to obtain some kind of explanation from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. McRae) as to why Connaught Laboratories have shown such a negative attitude toward an urgent request for a biological product which was so urgently needed by our fellow Commonwealth country, Malta.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul E. McRae (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-ALLEGED REFUSAL OF CONNAUGHT LABORATORIES TO SUPPLY GAMMA GLOBULIN TO MALTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) is certainly an important one. I am pleased that he has taken the action he has and that he has received a response from the Canadian Red Cross.
1 would like to give him the following brief explanation. After the hon. member's intervention in the House on March 4, the minister told his officials to investigate the matter immediately. According to Connaught Laboratories, the agent of Connaught in Malta was approached by Maltese officials in December to request the price of immune serum globulin. On February 3 an order was mailed by Maltese officials to Connaught Laboratories without explaining any urgency of the delivery of the order. Since it is common practice to submit a letter of credit with an order, Connaught Laboratories waited for the letter of credit. Although there was no urgency indicated in the order, 1 am informed that Connaught Laboratories decided to ship the 60 vials on March 8 regardless of the letter of credit because of the apparent urgency indicated by the hon. member. It was the hon. member's intervention which produced these results and also ensured the support of the Red Cross.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-ALLEGED NECESSITY OF SENDING PARACHUTES OF AIRBORNE REGIMENT FROM OTTAWA TO EDMONTON FOR REPACKING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as can be ascertained, no component of Air Command was consulted to examine the implications of the move of the Canadian Airborne Regiment from Edmonton, and the effect this would have on air operations in Edmonton, and the effect on air operations in Trenton. Associated with the air transport support implications will be a brand new series of costs associated with the transfer of the bulk of the Airborne Regiment from an all-weather air base to Canadian Forces Base Petawawa.
Adjournment Debate
In the light of what appears to be the latest decision not to move the airborne training facility and the parachute packing facility from Edmonton, it is clear that significant additional costs must be faced in terms of transporting personnel and cargo parachutes from Edmonton to eastern Canada and to increase the number of such parachutes to take the place of those that will be tied up in transportation east for use, and west for packing.
In addition, the joint training use of the C-130 Hercules aircraft of 435 Squadron when they are performing their own tactical air training will be impossible when the units are separated. In other words, the degree of close co-operative air training now possible when all units share a common air base will be impossible except at prohibitive expense with the split of the Airborne Regiment and its separation from the air base.
As a direct result of the move of the Canadian Airborne Regiment into Petawawa and Ottawa, there will be a requirement for significant new construction programs at both bases to provide adequate accommodation and training facilities. In addition, there will be a ripple effect on units in Ottawa and Petawawa that will be crowded into existing accommodation, or in the case of Petawawa some units may be forced to move to Gagetown, adding appreciably to the expenses connected with the replenishing of the Airborne Regiment.
In addition to the costs of the move, new and refurbished accommodation, new training areas, additional parachutes, additional and unknown transport support costs, there are the not inconsiderable costs associated with finding new and suitable drop zones, as the minister mentioned to the news media in North Bay. He is quoted as saying that North Bay is being considered as a jumping off point for their exercises and that North Bay, Trenton and Uplands are all being considered as transportation sites for the regiment. He said that the regiment would be trucked to one of these sites so they would board large aircraft to take them to deployment areas. Also to be considered are the additional costs in air transport hours to get exercises launched into the Canadian sub-Arctic and Arctic.
The most puzzling aspect of the entire redeployment plan for the Canadian Airborne Regiment lies in the fact that at no time has there been a clear and logical explanation of the military appreciation that led to such a questionable military decision. There is ample evidence to indicate that little or no consultation took place with the Air Command side, which in any airborne operation is probably the most important component in the airborne capability. In addition, there is considerable evidence to show that the current configuration of the Airborne Regiment has, for the first time in the history of the Canadian armed forces, led to the development of a truly effective land/air team which is capable of carrying out its operational missions effectively.
The puzzle to any objective military thinker or any informed layman is that on the surface there seems to be no military justification whatsoever for the move and separation of the Canadian Airborne Regiment.

March 10, 1977
Adjournment Debate

FARM CREDIT CORPORATION-ALLEGED DENIAL OF LOANS TO FARMERS GETTING LESS THAN FIFTY PER CENT OF INCOME FROM FARMING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I first raised the matter I raise this evening on November 29 last. The question relates to a young farmer who wishes to obtain a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation. I asked the Minister

of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) the following question, as reported at page 1454 of Hansard for November 29:
Is it government policy that the Farm Credit Corporation should deny young farmers, who are temporarily employed and not necessarily getting 50 per cent of their income from farming, loans as a result of their extracurricular work in an effort to try to make ends meet?
At the same time, would he also indicate whether a father who is retiring would be denied a grant from the Small Loans Assistance Program . . .
Mr. Speaker ruled the question as not acceptable. I rose on a point of order, in which I tried to elaborate on the matter, but Mr. Speaker again denied me the right to pursue it. I then took it upon myself to write to the Farm Credit Corporation about the matter I raised. The Corporation wrote back to me.
Before dealing with that, let me tell the House some of the circumstances of the case. A young man wanted to apply for a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation. He had been farming the land in question for two years. His father had retired and was receiving the old age pension. This young farmer had been renting the land and the father offered to sell it to him on good terms. When the father went to the Farm Credit Corporation asking for a grant, he was told that he could not get it, but that if he sold the land to the provincial land bank, he could qualify. That was the gist of the response I received. I was not satisfied with it and took the matter up in the Standing Committee on Agriculture. Would you believe me, Mr. Speaker, when I tell you that the chairman allowed me only five minutes to put my case? How many questions can you ask in five minutes? How can you ferret out government policies in five minutes?
What is more, five minutes ago I saw the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) behind the curtain. But the Minister of Agriculture is not in the Chamber opposite me, to answer my inquiry this evening. He will delegate that obligation to someone else. Mr. Speaker, this involves a matter of policy. I do not want to hear a lot of words or phrases. I want to hear some clarification of the policy. It is not good enough to hand me a lot of junk, as he did the other day. When discussing matters pertaining to the secretary of agriculture in the United States, he handed me a bunch of junk to do with storage.
I asked if that boy could get a loan, and why that father could not get a grant, if it was available and if he sold the land directly to his son. 1 also asked the minister in the Standing Committee on Agriculture whether he was in favour of state owned land. He said, no; yet he is not here to answer my question.
I have a letter from a branch manager of the Farm Credit Corporation which reads in part, and I quote:
That is why a vendor is not eligible for a grant unless he sells to someone who adds it to other land or sells it to the Saskatchewan Land Bank-
The minister cannot tell me he is not in favour of state owned land when the Farm Credit Corporation writes a letter like that to me.
March 10, 1977

I cannot get any information. I tried to get it this morning in the Agriculture Committee by continuing the questioning. Would you believe the chairman said he would allow me one question? Can you imagine that situation?
The minister ran out of the House. I do not want a secondhand answer from anyone who has been delegated. I have a right on behalf of that young man to know the government's policy. If I cannot get that information in the House or in the Committee discussing the estimates, I do not want someone else giving me a bunch of junk such as statistics about how many loans were made, in what areas, for what purpose, and so on.
I want to know the policy. I cannot get it from somebody who has been delegated. It has to be from the minister. Only a minister can enunciate policy as far as the government is concerned. It is a futile effort to try to get information from this government.
The minister was here five minutes ago. It is a shame that he could not stay. I warned him in committee about the
Adjournment Debate
question I would raise tonight. For him to tell me that he is not in favour of state owned land is a lot of baloney. He pulls manure wagons all over the country and he wants me to believe that he is in favour of small farms.
